items.question: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol, C2H5OH(l)? A 2C(g) + 6H(g) + O(g) -> C2H5OH(l), B 2C(s) + 3H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> C2H5OH(l), C 2C(s) + 6H(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> C2H5OH(l), D C2H4(g) + H2O(l) -> C2H5OH(l).
steps: Enthalpy change of formation is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states.
Carbon is solid (graphite), hydrogen and oxygen are diatomic gases, so the reactants are 2C(s), 3H2(g) and 1/2O2(g): option B.
A and C start from gaseous atoms, which are not the standard states of the elements; D forms ethanol from two compounds, not from elements.

items.question: 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution in an insulated cup. The temperature rises by 13.7 K. Assume that the mixture has density 1.00 g cm⁻³ and specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K^-1. What is the enthalpy change of neutralisation? A -28.6 kJ mol⁻¹, B -2.86 kJ mol⁻¹, C -57.3 kJ mol⁻¹, D +57.3 kJ mol^-1.
items.answer: C: -57.3 kJ mol⁻¹
steps: Mass of solution = 50.0 g, so q = m c Delta T = 50.0 x 4.18 x 13.7 = 2863 J = 2.86 kJ.
Moles of HCl (and of NaOH) = 0.0250 x 2.00 = 0.0500 mol, so Delta H = -2.86 / 0.0500 = -57.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative because the temperature rises).
A uses a mass of 25.0 g instead of 50.0 g; B forgets to divide by the moles; D has the wrong sign for an exothermic reaction.

items.question: Define the term standard enthalpy change of combustion.
items.answer: The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with all reactants and products in their standard states
steps: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is burned completely in (excess) oxygen
Under standard conditions (a pressure of 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K), with all reactants and products in their standard states
accept: Reacts fully / completely with oxygen, in place of "burned completely"
Standard pressure given as 1 bar (100 kPa)
Complete combustion to the oxides, for example CO2(g) and H2O(l) for an organic compound
Temperature of 298 K (25 C) stated

items.question: Calculate the standard enthalpy change of formation of propanone, CH3COCH3(l), using the standard enthalpy changes of combustion: C(s) = -394 kJ mol⁻¹, H2(g) = -286 kJ mol⁻¹, CH3COCH3(l) = -1790 kJ mol^-1.
items.answer: -250 kJ mol⁻¹
steps: Formation equation: 3C(s) + 3H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> CH3COCH3(l).
Hess cycle: the elements and propanone both burn to give 3CO2(g) + 3H2O(l), so Delta fH = sum of Delta cH(reactants) - Delta cH(propanone).
Delta fH(propanone) = -250 kJ mol⁻¹

items.question: In an experiment, 0.583 g of propan-1-ol, C3H7OH (M = 60.0 g mol⁻¹), was burned and the energy transferred to the water was 17.2 kJ. Calculate the experimental enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol, giving your answer to 3 significant figures with a sign and units.
items.answer: -1770 kJ mol⁻¹
steps: Moles of propan-1-ol = 0.583 / 60.0 = 0.00972 mol.
Energy released per mole = 17.2 / 0.00972 = 1770 kJ mol^-1.
Combustion is exothermic, so Delta cH = -1770 kJ mol^-1.

steps: Two readings are used to find the temperature rise, so the uncertainty in the rise is 2 x 0.5 = +/- 1.0 K.

items.question: Calculate the standard enthalpy change for the hydrogenation of cyclohexene, C6H10(l) + H2(g) -> C6H12(l), using the standard enthalpy changes of combustion: cyclohexene = -3752 kJ mol⁻¹, cyclohexane = -3920 kJ mol⁻¹, hydrogen = -286 kJ mol^-1.
items.answer: -118 kJ mol⁻¹

Delta H = Delta cH(C6H10) + Delta cH(H2) - Delta cH(C6H12) = (-3752) + (-286) - (-3920).

items.question: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene, C6H10 + H2 -> C6H12, is -118 kJ mol^-1. The measured enthalpy change for the hydrogenation of benzene, C6H6(l) + 3H2(g) -> C6H12(l), is -205 kJ mol^-1. Calculate the value expected for benzene if it contained three separate C=C bonds like the one in cyclohexene, and the difference between this and the measured value.
items.answer: Expected -354 kJ mol⁻¹; the measured value is 149 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic
steps: Three C=C bonds would each be hydrogenated with -118 kJ mol⁻¹: 3 x (-118) = -354 kJ mol⁻¹ (1 mark).
Measured value is -205 kJ mol⁻¹ (1 mark).
Difference = -205 - (-354) = +149 kJ mol⁻¹: benzene releases 149 kJ mol⁻¹ less energy than expected (1 mark).

items.question: The measured enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene is 149 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic than the value expected for three separate C=C bonds. Deduce what this shows about the structure of benzene.
items.answer: Benzene is more stable than a ring of three localised C=C bonds, because its pi electrons are delocalised
steps: Benzene is more stable (lower in energy) than the hypothetical molecule with three localised C=C bonds, because it releases less energy when hydrogenated
Benzene has delocalised pi electrons round the ring, so it does not contain three separate C=C double bonds
accept: The delocalisation stabilises benzene by about 149 kJ mol⁻¹
All the carbon-carbon bonds in benzene are the same length, between the length of a single bond and a double bond
The Kekule structure with alternating single and double bonds is not a correct model of benzene

items.question: The enthalpy change for the reaction CH4(g) -> C(g) + 4H(g) is +1664 kJ mol^-1. What is the mean bond enthalpy of the C-H bond in methane? A +555 kJ mol⁻¹, B +416 kJ mol⁻¹, C +1664 kJ mol⁻¹, D +6656 kJ mol^-1.
items.answer: B: +416 kJ mol⁻¹
steps: The reaction breaks four C-H bonds, so the mean bond enthalpy = 1664 / 4 = +416 kJ mol^-1.
A divides by 3 instead of 4; C is the energy for all four bonds; D multiplies by 4 instead of dividing.

items.question: Use the mean bond enthalpies C=C 612, C-C 347, C-H 413 and H-H 436 (all in kJ mol⁻¹) to find the enthalpy change for C2H4(g) + H2(g) -> C2H6(g). A +125 kJ mol⁻¹, B +288 kJ mol⁻¹, C -125 kJ mol⁻¹, D -1173 kJ mol^-1.
items.answer: C: -125 kJ mol⁻¹
steps: Bonds broken: C=C + H-H = 612 + 436 = 1048 kJ mol^-1.
Bonds made: C-C + 2 C-H = 347 + 826 = 1173 kJ mol^-1.
Delta H = 1048 - 1173 = -125 kJ mol^-1. A has the wrong sign, B counts only one C-H bond made, D is the energy of the bonds made only.

items.question: Define the term mean bond enthalpy.
items.answer: The enthalpy change to break 1 mol of a covalent bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over a range of different compounds
steps: The enthalpy change when one mole of a covalent bond is broken, with the molecules in the gaseous state (gaseous molecules to gaseous atoms)
The value is an average taken over a variety of compounds containing that bond
accept: Energy required to break one mole of bonds in the gaseous state, averaged over different molecules
Mean (average) of the bond dissociation enthalpies of that bond in different environments
The enthalpy change for X-Y(g) -> X(g) + Y(g), averaged over a range of compounds

items.question: Show that the mean bond enthalpy of the O-H bond is about +463 kJ mol⁻¹, using the enthalpy change of formation of water vapour, H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> H2O(g), Delta H = -241.8 kJ mol⁻¹, and the bond enthalpies H-H = +436 kJ mol⁻¹ and O=O = +498 kJ mol^-1.
steps: Bonds broken: 1 H-H and 1/2 O=O = 436 + 249 = 685 kJ mol^-1.
Bonds made: 2 O-H bonds = 2E(O-H).
Delta H = bonds broken - bonds made, so -241.8 = 685 - 2E(O-H).

items.answer: Mean bond enthalpies are averages; the experimental value is for liquid water (condensation releases energy)
steps: Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so they are not exact for the bonds in propane, CO2 and H2O
The experimental value is for liquid water but the calculation uses gaseous water; condensing 4 mol of water releases extra energy
accept: Bond enthalpies refer to gaseous species, whereas the experimental value refers to standard states (liquid water at 298 K)
The C-C, C-H and O-H bond enthalpies are averages that differ slightly from the actual values in propane and water

items.question: Explain why a bond enthalpy calculation would give a less reliable value of Delta H for the dehydration of liquid ethanol than for gaseous ethanol.
items.answer: Mean bond enthalpies apply to gaseous molecules; for a liquid, energy is also needed to overcome intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds), which the calculation ignores
steps: Mean bond enthalpies are defined for bonds in gaseous molecules
Liquid ethanol has hydrogen bonds and other intermolecular forces; the extra energy to separate the molecules (vaporise the liquid) is not included in the bond enthalpy calculation
accept: The enthalpy change of vaporisation of ethanol would have to be added to the calculated value
The bond enthalpy of O-H in liquid ethanol differs from the mean value because of hydrogen bonding
The product water would be liquid, not gaseous, so its condensation also has to be allowed for

items.question: The mean bond enthalpies of C-Cl, C-Br and C-I are +346, +290 and +228 kJ mol^-1. Explain, in terms of bond enthalpy, why 1-iodobutane is hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide faster than 1-chlorobutane under the same conditions.
items.answer: The C-I bond is the weakest, so it needs the least energy to break, giving the lowest activation energy and the fastest reaction
steps: The C-I bond has the lowest bond enthalpy (+228 kJ mol⁻¹) so it is the weakest of the three bonds
Less energy is needed to break the C-I bond, so the activation energy of the hydrolysis is lower
A greater proportion of collisions has at least the activation energy, so the rate is faster
accept: C-I bond is longer and the bonding electrons are further from the nucleus, so the bond is weaker
The rate-determining step involves breaking the carbon-halogen bond
The C-Cl bond (+346 kJ mol⁻¹) is the strongest, so chlorobutane is hydrolysed most slowly

items.question: Which equation represents the lattice energy of magnesium oxide? A Mg2+(g) + O2-(g) -> MgO(s); B Mg(s) + 1/2O2(g) -> MgO(s); C Mg2+(aq) + O2-(aq) -> MgO(s); D MgO(s) -> Mg2+(g) + O2-(g).
items.answer: A: Mg2+(g) + O2-(g) -> MgO(s)
steps: Lattice energy is defined as the enthalpy change when 1 mol of an ionic solid forms from its gaseous ions, so it is exothermic.
B is the enthalpy change of formation, C uses aqueous ions, and D is the reverse process (lattice dissociation enthalpy).

items.question: Which compound is predicted to have the most exothermic lattice energy? A LiF, B NaCl, C CaS, D MgO.
items.answer: D: MgO
steps: Lattice energy becomes more exothermic as the ionic charges increase and as the ionic radii decrease.
MgO and CaS both contain 2+ and 2- ions, so they are more exothermic than LiF and NaCl.
Mg2+ and O2- are smaller than Ca2+ and S2-, so the ions in MgO are closer together and attract more strongly: D.

items.answer: -122 kJ mol⁻¹
steps: Energy cycle: MgCl2(s) -> Mg2+(g) + 2Cl-(g) is the reverse of the lattice energy, so +2526 kJ mol^-1.
Then hydrate the gaseous ions: -1920 + 2(-364) = -2648 kJ mol^-1.

items.question: Explain why the lattice energy of magnesium oxide, MgO, is more exothermic than the lattice energy of calcium oxide, CaO.
items.answer: Mg2+ is smaller than Ca2+, so it has a higher charge density and attracts O2- more strongly
steps: Both oxides contain ions with the same charges, 2+ and 2-, so the difference comes from the ionic radii
Mg2+ is smaller than Ca2+ (one fewer electron shell), so the ions are closer together and the charge density of the cation is higher
The electrostatic attraction between the ions in MgO is stronger, so more energy is released when the lattice forms
accept: Distance between the nuclei of the ions is smaller in MgO
Lattice energy depends on the charges on the ions and the sum of the ionic radii
MgO has the more exothermic lattice energy because the ionic bonding is stronger

items.question: Use the following data to calculate the lattice energy of calcium oxide, CaO. Enthalpy change of formation of CaO = -635 kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy change of atomisation of calcium = +178 kJ mol⁻¹; first ionisation energy of calcium = +590 kJ mol⁻¹; second ionisation energy of calcium = +1145 kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy change of atomisation of oxygen, 1/2O2(g) -> O(g) = +249 kJ mol⁻¹; first electron affinity of oxygen = -141 kJ mol⁻¹; second electron affinity of oxygen = +798 kJ mol^-1.
items.answer: -3454 kJ mol⁻¹
steps: Hess's law: Delta fH = Delta atH(Ca) + IE1 + IE2 + Delta atH(O) + EA1 + EA2 + lattice energy (1 mark for a correct cycle or expression).
Sum of the terms other than the lattice energy = 178 + 590 + 1145 + 249 + (-141) + 798 (1 mark for all six terms with correct signs).
This sum = +2819 kJ mol⁻¹ (1 mark).
Lattice energy = -635 - 2819 = -3454 kJ mol⁻¹ (1 mark).

items.question: Explain why the second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic, whereas the first electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic.
items.answer: The O- ion is negatively charged and repels the incoming electron, so energy must be supplied
steps: The first electron is added to a neutral atom and is attracted by the nucleus, so energy is released (exothermic)
The second electron is added to a negative ion, O-, which repels it; energy must be supplied to force the electron on (endothermic)
accept: Repulsion between the negative ion and the incoming electron outweighs the attraction to the nucleus
The energy released when the O2- lattice forms (the lattice energy) compensates for the endothermic second electron affinity
Second electron affinity is positive because the electron is added to an ion with a negative charge

items.answer: The two values are similar (within about 2%), so CaO is almost completely ionic with very little covalent character
steps: The Born-Haber value (-3454 kJ mol⁻¹) is only slightly more exothermic than the ionic-model value (-3401 kJ mol⁻¹), a difference of about 1.6%
The ionic model, which assumes perfectly spherical ions with purely electrostatic attraction, fits well, so calcium oxide is almost purely ionic
accept: The small difference suggests a small degree of covalent character because Ca2+ slightly polarises the O2- ion
The experimental (Born-Haber) value being more exothermic than the ionic-model value means the ionic model slightly underestimates the attraction
A large difference would show significant covalent character

items.question: The enthalpy change of formation of MgCl(s) is -94 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of MgCl2(s) is -643 kJ mol^-1. Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction 2MgCl(s) -> Mg(s) + MgCl2(s). Hence explain why magnesium forms MgCl2 and not MgCl, even though the formation of MgCl is exothermic.
items.answer: -455 kJ mol⁻¹; MgCl would change to Mg and MgCl2 exothermically, so MgCl is unstable
steps: Delta H = Delta fH(MgCl2) - 2 x Delta fH(MgCl) = -643 - 2(-94)
Delta H = -455 kJ mol⁻¹
The reaction is strongly exothermic, so MgCl is unstable with respect to Mg and MgCl2 (it would disproportionate) and is not formed
The large extra energy needed for the second ionisation energy of magnesium (+1451 kJ mol⁻¹) is more than repaid by the much more exothermic lattice energy of MgCl2 (2+ ion, stronger attraction)
accept: MgCl2 is thermodynamically more stable than MgCl relative to Mg and Cl2: -643 kJ mol⁻¹ compared with -94 kJ mol⁻¹
The lattice energy of MgCl2 (-2526 kJ mol⁻¹) is far more exothermic than that of MgCl (-753 kJ mol⁻¹) because Mg2+ has a higher charge and charge density than Mg+
Mg+ in MgCl is both oxidised (to Mg2+) and reduced (to Mg), so MgCl disproportionates

steps: Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T = -178 000 / 298 = -597.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (1 mark).

items.question: Explain why a reaction with a positive Delta H and a positive entropy change of the system can become feasible if the temperature is increased.
items.answer: Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T is negative but gets smaller in size as T rises, so Delta S total becomes positive
steps: Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T is negative for an endothermic reaction, but its size falls as T increases
Delta S system is positive and changes little with T, so above a certain temperature Delta S total = Delta S system + Delta S surroundings becomes positive and the reaction is feasible
accept: At high temperature the entropy increase of the system outweighs the entropy decrease of the surroundings
The minimum temperature is found when Delta S total = 0, that is T = Delta H / Delta S system

items.question: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water even though the process is endothermic and the temperature of the solution falls. Explain this in terms of entropy changes.
items.answer: Delta S system is positive and larger in size than the negative Delta S surroundings, so Delta S total is positive
steps: The ordered crystal lattice breaks up into free ions in solution, so the entropy of the system increases (Delta S system is positive)
The process is endothermic: energy is taken from the surroundings, so the entropy of the surroundings decreases (Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T is negative)
Delta S total = Delta S system + Delta S surroundings
The increase in entropy of the system is larger than the decrease in entropy of the surroundings, so Delta S total is positive and dissolving is feasible
accept: The ions in solution are free to move, giving many more ways of arranging the particles and the energy
The size of Delta S surroundings is small because Delta H is small (+25.7 kJ mol⁻¹)
The reaction is feasible (spontaneous) because Delta S total is greater than zero, even though Delta H is positive
Quoting Delta S total = +22.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, from (a), as evidence

items.question: The reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g) has a negative Delta H and a negative entropy change of the system. The reaction CH4(g) + H2O(g) -> CO(g) + 3H2(g) has a positive Delta H and a positive entropy change of the system. Discuss how a change in temperature affects the feasibility of each reaction, using Delta S total = Delta S system - Delta H / T.
items.answer: Ammonia synthesis is feasible at low temperature but not at high temperature; steam reforming is feasible only at high temperature
steps: Ammonia synthesis: Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T is positive, but Delta S system is negative
At low temperature Delta S surroundings is large, so Delta S total is positive and the reaction is feasible
As T increases Delta S surroundings gets smaller, so above T = Delta H / Delta S system, Delta S total is negative and the reaction is not feasible
Steam reforming: Delta S system is positive, but Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T is negative
At low temperature Delta S surroundings is large and negative, so Delta S total is negative and the reaction is not feasible
As T increases Delta S surroundings becomes smaller in size, so above T = Delta H / Delta S system, Delta S total is positive and the reaction is feasible
accept: Delta S system is negative for ammonia synthesis because 4 mol of gas form 2 mol of gas; it is positive for steam reforming because 2 mol of gas form 4 mol of gas
The changeover temperature is where Delta S total = 0, that is T = Delta H / Delta S system
Feasibility says nothing about rate: a feasible reaction may be very slow without a catalyst
Delta S total must be greater than (or equal to) zero for a reaction to be feasible

items.question: The rate of a reaction approximately doubles when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 310 K. Explain, with reference to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies, why a small rise in temperature has such a large effect on the rate.
items.answer: At higher temperature many more molecules have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so many more collisions are successful
steps: At the higher temperature the distribution curve shifts to higher energy (the peak is lower and further right); the area under the curve is unchanged because the number of molecules is the same
The high-energy tail rises sharply, so the proportion of molecules with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy increases by a large factor (the activation energy itself is unchanged)
A much greater fraction of collisions is successful, so the rate increases (here it roughly doubles)
accept: Molecules also have a higher mean kinetic energy, move faster and collide more often, but this is a much smaller effect than the change in the fraction with enough energy
The activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a collision to be successful
The area under the curve to the right of the activation energy is much larger at the higher temperature
The fraction of molecules with energy of at least the activation energy depends exponentially on temperature

items.answer: The steps add to give NO2 + CO -> NO + CO2; the slow step 1 involves two NO2 and no CO, so rate = k[NO2]²
steps: Adding the steps: 2NO2 + NO3 + CO -> NO3 + NO + NO2 + CO2; cancelling NO3 and one NO2 gives NO2 + CO -> NO + CO2
Step 1 is the slow, rate-determining step and it involves two NO2 molecules, so the rate depends on [NO2]²
CO takes part only in the fast step after the rate-determining step, so the rate does not depend on [CO] (zero order)
accept: NO3 is an intermediate: it is formed in step 1 and used up in step 2, so it does not appear in the overall equation
The rate equation contains only the species that react in the rate-determining step (and anything before it)
The powers in the rate equation match the number of molecules of each species in the slow step

items.question: Sulfur trioxide is made in the Contact process: 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g), Delta H = -197 kJ mol^-1. The reaction is carried out at about 450 C and a pressure of 100 to 200 kPa, using a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst. items.answer: Compromise conditions: moderate temperature and low pressure give a high enough yield at a good rate, and the catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the yield
steps: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield
But a low temperature makes the rate too slow, so 450 C is a compromise that gives an acceptable rate and a high yield
There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so a high pressure would increase the yield
The yield is already high at 100 to 200 kPa, so a high pressure is not worth the extra cost of equipment and energy, or the safety risks
The catalyst provides a route with a lower activation energy, so the reaction is fast enough at a moderate temperature (saving energy cost)
The catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield, only the time taken to reach equilibrium
accept: A higher temperature would favour the endothermic (reverse) direction, so the equilibrium would move to the left and the yield would fall
A higher temperature increases the rate because a greater proportion of molecules has energy of at least the activation energy
High pressure needs thick-walled pipes and compressors, which are expensive to build and run
The catalyst is not used up, so it can be reused, which keeps costs down

items.question: The pH of human blood is kept close to 7.4 by a buffer system containing carbonic acid, H2CO3, and hydrogencarbonate ions, HCO3-. Explain how this buffer limits the change in pH when lactic acid enters the blood during exercise, and when a small amount of alkali enters the blood.
items.answer: Added H+ reacts with HCO3-, shifting the equilibrium to H2CO3; added OH- reacts with H+ and H2CO3 dissociates to replace it
steps: The equilibrium is H2CO3 <=> H+ + HCO3-; the blood contains large amounts of both the weak acid H2CO3 and its conjugate base HCO3-
When lactic acid is added, the extra H+ reacts with HCO3-: H+ + HCO3- -> H2CO3, so the equilibrium moves to the left
The concentration of HCO3- is large compared with the amount of H+ added, so the ratio [H2CO3] / [HCO3-] changes only slightly and the pH stays almost constant
When alkali is added, OH- reacts with H+: H+ + OH- -> H2O
More H2CO3 dissociates to replace the H+ removed (the equilibrium moves to the right), so the ratio changes little and the pH changes only slightly
accept: [H+] = Ka x [H2CO3] / [HCO3-], so the pH depends on the ratio of the two concentrations, which changes very little
Added OH- may be shown reacting directly with H2CO3: OH- + H2CO3 -> HCO3- + H2O
The buffer is effective because the weak acid and its conjugate base are both present in large amounts
Le Chatelier: the equilibrium moves to oppose each change

items.question: A salt dissolves in water with an enthalpy change of solution of +12 kJ mol⁻¹ and an entropy change of the system of +110 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Which statement is correct? A The salt cannot dissolve because the process is endothermic, B The entropy change of the surroundings is +40.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, C The total entropy change is -40.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so dissolving is not feasible, D The total entropy change is +69.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so dissolving is feasible.
items.answer: D: the total entropy change is +69.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so dissolving is feasible
steps: Delta S surroundings = -Delta H / T = -12 000 / 298 = -40.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (the process is endothermic).
Delta S total = +110 + (-40.3) = +69.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; a positive total means that dissolving is feasible.
A ignores the entropy increase of the system; B has the wrong sign for Delta S surroundings; C ignores Delta S system.

Acid prevents a white precipitate of barium carbonate (or barium sulfite) forming, which would give a false positive

C12.19 - use entropy and enthalpy cha
items.question: The enthalpy change of solution of calcium sulfate is exothermic, about -18 kJ mol⁻¹, but calcium sulfate is only sparingly soluble in water. Suggest an explanation in terms of entropy changes.
items.answer: The entropy of the system decreases because the highly charged ions order the water molecules, so the total entropy change is small or negative
steps: The process is exothermic, so the entropy change of the surroundings is positive (-Delta H / T)
Ca2+ and SO4²- ions have high charge densities and attract water molecules strongly, so water molecules become more ordered in the hydration shells and the entropy of the system decreases
This decrease largely or completely cancels the positive entropy change of the surroundings, so the total entropy change is small or negative and little calcium sulfate dissolves
accept: Delta S surroundings is about +60 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (18 000 / 298), which is outweighed by a larger negative Delta S system
Delta S total must be greater than zero for dissolving to be feasible
The two ions are each doubly charged (2+ and 2-), so more water molecules are held in an ordered arrangement than for singly charged ions

items.question: The solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group from magnesium sulfate to barium sulfate. Explain this trend in terms of the lattice energy and the enthalpy change of hydration of the ions.
items.answer: The hydration enthalpy of the cation becomes less exothermic by more than the lattice energy does, so the enthalpy change of solution becomes less exothermic
steps: The enthalpy change of solution = -(lattice energy) + the sum of the enthalpy changes of hydration of the ions; a less exothermic value means a less soluble sulfate
Down the group the cations get larger, so the charge density of the cation falls
The enthalpy change of hydration of the cation becomes less exothermic, as the attraction to water molecules is weaker

The lattice energy also becomes less exothermic, but by a smaller amount, because the sulfate ion is large compared with all of the cations, so the change in cation size has little effect on the ion separation
So the hydration enthalpy becomes less exothermic by more than the lattice energy does, the enthalpy change of solution becomes less exothermic (more endothermic) and the solubility decreases
accept: Mg2+ has the highest charge density, so MgSO4 has the most exothermic hydration enthalpy and is the most soluble
Barium sulfate is the least soluble sulfate in the group
Both ions in the lattice are doubly charged, so the lattice energy is large for every sulfate, but it varies little with the cation
Ionic radius of the cation increases down the group

steps: HBr adds across the C=C by electrophilic addition: H+ bonds to one alkene carbon and Br- to the other.

items.question: 1-bromobutane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide mainly by the SN2 mechanism, but 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts mainly by the SN1 mechanism. items.answer: Primary 1-bromobutane: unhindered, one-step SN2, rate = k[RBr][OH-]. Tertiary 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: hindered but gives a stable carbocation, two-step SN1, rate = k[RBr].
steps: 1-bromobutane is a primary halogenoalkane: the carbon bonded to Br is not crowded, so OH- can attack it directly from the side opposite the Br (1 mark).
A primary carbocation would be unstable, so SN2 occurs in one step through a transition state in which OH- is partly bonded to carbon as the C-Br bond breaks (1 mark).
In SN2 both the halogenoalkane and OH- are involved in the rate-determining step, so rate = k[C4H9Br][OH-]: second order overall (1 mark).
2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary: the three CH3 groups block attack by OH-, and electron-releasing alkyl groups stabilise the carbocation (CH3)3C+ (1 mark).
The C-Br bond breaks first in a slow step to give (CH3)3C+ and Br-, then OH- attacks quickly. Rate = k[(CH3)3CBr]: first order and independent of [OH-] (1 mark).

items.question: Ethanol is made by fermentation of glucose and by the hydration of ethene. Evaluate the use of fermentation compared with hydration of ethene for the large-scale production of ethanol, considering the raw materials, the reaction conditions, the type of process and the purity of the product.
items.answer: Fermentation is renewable and uses mild conditions but is slow, batch and gives dilute ethanol with a 51% atom economy; hydration is fast, continuous, pure and 100% atom economic but uses finite crude oil and high temperature and pressure.
steps: Raw materials: fermentation uses sugars from plants, which are renewable; hydration uses ethene from crude oil, which is finite.
Conditions: fermentation works at about 30-40 °C and atmospheric pressure, so it needs little energy; hydration needs about 300 °C and 60-70 atm, which is energy intensive.
Type of process: fermentation is slow and a batch process; hydration is fast and continuous, giving a high output.
Product: fermentation gives a dilute ethanol solution that needs fractional distillation; hydration gives a purer product, with atom economy of 100% against 51% for fermentation.
Any four of these points earn the 4 marks, including a reasoned overall judgement, for example that fermentation is more sustainable but hydration is more efficient and economic at large scale.

items.question: Ethanal, CH3CHO, reacts with hydrogen cyanide to form 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH3CH(OH)CN. State the type of reaction and explain why the carbon atom of the C=O group in ethanal is attacked by the cyanide ion.
items.answer: Nucleophilic addition; the C=O carbon is delta+ because oxygen is more electronegative, so it is attacked by the nucleophile CN-.
steps: The reaction is nucleophilic addition: CN- adds across the C=O double bond.
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar and the carbon is delta+.
CN- is a nucleophile (it donates a lone pair of electrons), so it attacks the electron-deficient carbon atom.

items.question: Ethanal reacts with cyanide ions and acid to form 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH3CH(OH)CN, whose molecules are chiral. Explain why the product made in this reaction has no effect on plane-polarised light.
items.answer: The planar C=O is attacked from either side with equal probability, so equal amounts of the two enantiomers form (a racemic mixture) and their effects on plane-polarised light cancel.
steps: CH3CH(OH)CN has a chiral centre: the carbon bonded to four different groups (H, CH3, OH and CN).
The C=O group and the atoms bonded to it are planar, so CN- can attack from above or below the plane with equal probability.
Equal amounts of the two non-superimposable mirror-image forms (enantiomers) form, a racemic mixture. Their rotations of plane-polarised light cancel, so the mixture is optically inactive.

items.question: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene to cyclohexane is -120 kJ mol^-1. The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane is -208 kJ mol^-1. Compared with a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene that has three localised C=C bonds, benzene is A 152 kJ mol⁻¹ less stable, B 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable, C 88 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable, D 240 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable.
items.answer: B: benzene is 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable
steps: If benzene had three localised C=C bonds, hydrogenation would release about 3 x (-120) = -360 kJ mol^-1.
The measured value is -208 kJ mol⁻¹, which is 360 - 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic.
Less energy is released because benzene starts at a lower energy, so benzene is 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable owing to delocalisation (B).
A has the sign reversed. C comes from 208 - 120 and D from 360 - 120, which are both invalid comparisons.

items.question: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride to form phenylethanone, C6H5COCH3. Which species is the electrophile that attacks the benzene ring? A CH3COCl, B CH3CO+, C Cl+, D AlCl4-.
items.answer: B: CH3CO+
steps: Aluminium chloride accepts a lone pair from the chlorine of ethanoyl chloride: CH3COCl + AlCl3 -> CH3CO+ + AlCl4-.
CH3CO+ is positively charged and electron deficient, so it attacks the delocalised pi electrons of the ring: it is the electrophile (B).
CH3COCl (A) is the reactant, not the attacking species. Cl+ (C) is not formed in this reaction. AlCl4- (D) is the negative ion that later removes H+ and regenerates AlCl3.

items.question: Benzene is nitrated by a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at about 50 °C. (i) Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile in this mixture. (ii) Explain why the sulfuric acid is described as a catalyst. (iii) Give a reason why the temperature must not rise much above 55 °C.
items.answer: (i) HNO3 + H2SO4 -> NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O; (ii) it is regenerated in the final step (H+ + HSO4- -> H2SO4); (iii) above 55 °C further nitration gives dinitrobenzene.
steps: (i) The electrophile is the nitronium ion: HNO3 + H2SO4 -> NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O (1 mark).
(ii) The H+ lost from the ring in the last step reacts with HSO4-: H+ + HSO4- -> H2SO4, so the sulfuric acid is regenerated and is not used up (1 mark).
(iii) At higher temperatures a second NO2 group is substituted, giving dinitrobenzene as an unwanted product (1 mark).

items.question: Phenol reacts with aqueous bromine at room temperature, but benzene does not react with bromine under the same conditions. State what is seen when excess bromine water is added to phenol and explain the difference in reactivity.
items.answer: The bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms; the lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, making it more electron rich and more reactive than benzene.
steps: Observation: the orange bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms (1 mark).
In phenol a lone pair on the oxygen atom overlaps with and is delocalised into the pi system of the ring, increasing the electron density of the ring, especially at positions 2, 4 and 6 (1 mark).

The more electron-rich ring polarises Br2 more strongly, so substitution occurs without a halogen carrier. Benzene has a lower electron density, so it needs a catalyst such as FeBr3 or AlBr3 (1 mark).

items.question: Cyclohexene decolourises bromine water at room temperature by addition, but benzene reacts with bromine only in the presence of a halogen carrier such as iron(III) bromide, and it gives a substitution product. Explain these differences in terms of the structure and bonding in the two molecules.
items.answer: Cyclohexene has a localised, electron-rich C=C that polarises Br2; benzene has delocalised pi electrons, so it needs a halogen carrier to make a stronger electrophile and it undergoes substitution to keep the delocalised ring.
steps: In cyclohexene the pi electrons are localised between two carbon atoms, giving a high electron density that polarises Br2, so no catalyst is needed (1 mark).
In benzene the six pi electrons are delocalised over the whole ring, so the electron density between any two carbons is lower and benzene cannot polarise Br2 enough to react (1 mark).
A halogen carrier (FeBr3 or AlBr3) accepts a lone pair from Br2 to generate a much stronger electrophile, Br+ (1 mark).
Addition to benzene would destroy the delocalised system and lose its extra stability of about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ (1 mark).
Substitution of H by Br keeps the delocalised ring, giving bromobenzene and HBr (1 mark).

items.question: Which compound is the strongest base? A ammonia, NH3, B ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2, C phenylamine, C6H5NH2, D ethanamide, CH3CONH2.
items.answer: B: ethylamine
steps: Basic strength depends on how available the lone pair on nitrogen is to accept H+.
In ethylamine the electron-releasing ethyl group increases the electron density on N, so its lone pair accepts H+ more readily than the lone pair in ammonia.
In phenylamine the lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring, and in ethanamide it is delocalised towards the C=O group, so both are much weaker bases than ammonia.

A heat with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube, B heat under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide and then reduce the product with LiAlH4 in dry ether, C heat under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide and then heat the product under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid, D heat under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide and then react the product with ammonia.

items.answer: Ethylamine is also a nucleophile, so it reacts with more bromoethane; use a large excess of ammonia.

items.answer: Step 1: HBr gives CH3CH2Br. Step 2: KCN in aqueous ethanol, heat under reflux, gives CH3CH2CN. Step 3: dilute HCl, heat under reflux, gives CH3CH2COOH.
steps: Step 1: ethene and hydrogen bromide (room temperature) by electrophilic addition give bromoethane, CH3CH2Br.
Step 2: heat under reflux with potassium cyanide in aqueous ethanol (nucleophilic substitution) to give propanenitrile, CH3CH2CN. This step adds the extra carbon atom.
Step 3: heat under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid (or sulfuric acid) to hydrolyse the nitrile to propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH.
One mark for each correct step and one mark for correct organic products at each stage (4 marks in total).

items.question: A sample containing only one optical isomer of 2-bromobutane, CH3CHBrCH2CH3, is hydrolysed to butan-2-ol with aqueous potassium hydroxide. Explain how the optical activity of the butan-2-ol formed would differ if the reaction took place entirely by (i) the SN1 mechanism and (ii) the SN2 mechanism.
items.answer: SN1: planar carbocation attacked from either side gives a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive. SN2: attack from the side opposite Br gives a single enantiomer (inverted configuration), which is optically active.
steps: SN1: the C-Br bond breaks first to give a planar carbocation intermediate, CH3CH+CH2CH3 (1 mark).

OH- can attack the planar carbocation from either side with equal probability, so equal amounts of the two enantiomers form (a racemic mixture) (1 mark). The effects on plane-polarised light cancel, so the product is optically inactive.
SN2: OH- attacks the carbon from the side opposite Br in a single step, so the configuration at the chiral carbon is inverted (1 mark).
Only one enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms, so the product remains optically active (1 mark).

items.answer: W is butanone, CH3COCH2CH3

The yellow precipitate (CHI3) with iodine and sodium hydroxide shows that W contains the CH3C=O group (1 mark).
The only ketone with formula C4H8O is butanone, CH3COCH2CH3, which does contain a CH3C=O group (1 mark).

items.question: Compound E is an ester with the molecular formula C4H8O2. Its high-resolution 1H NMR spectrum has three peaks: a singlet at 3.7 ppm (relative area 3), a quartet at 2.3 ppm (relative area 2) and a triplet at 1.1 ppm (relative area 3). [Chemical shifts: CH3-C 0.9-1.3 ppm; CH2-C=O 2.1-2.7 ppm; CH3-O 3.3-4.3 ppm.] Deduce the structure of E, explaining the splitting of the quartet and the triplet.
items.answer: Methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3
steps: Singlet at 3.7 ppm, area 3: a CH3 group bonded to oxygen (OCH3) with no hydrogens on the adjacent atom.

Triplet at 1.1 ppm, area 3: a CH3 group split into three by the two hydrogens of the neighbouring CH2 (n + 1 = 3). The fragments CH3CH2-, -COO- and -CH3 give CH3CH2COOCH3, methyl propanoate.

items.question: State and explain the trend in electronegativity across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine.
items.answer: Electronegativity increases because the nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases, so the bonding pair is attracted more strongly
steps: Electronegativity increases from sodium to chlorine
The nuclear charge increases and the atomic radius decreases (shielding is about constant)
So the nucleus attracts the bonding pair of electrons more strongly

the effective nuclear charge increases
the outer shell stays the same (n = 3), so the shielding is about constant

items.question: The electrical conductivity of the metals increases in the order sodium, magnesium, aluminium. Explain this trend.
items.answer: The number of delocalised electrons per atom increases (1, 2, 3), so more charge carriers move through the metal
steps: Metals conduct because delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice
Each Na atom provides 1 delocalised electron, each Mg atom 2 and each Al atom 3
There are more charge carriers per unit volume from Na to Al, so the conductivity increases
accept: delocalised electrons carry the charge when a potential difference is applied
the electron density in the metal lattice increases from Na to Al

items.question: In which reaction is the organic product optically active? propanal reacting with HCN in the presence of KCN propanone reacting with HCN in the presence of KCN a single enantiomer of 2-chlorobutane reacting with aqueous hydroxide ions by an SN2 mechanism a single enantiomer of 3-chloro-3-methylheptane reacting with water by an SN1 mechanism

D: the planar carbocation is attacked equally from both sides, giving a racemic mixture.

items.question: A chemist used rate data and optical activity to investigate the mechanisms of three reactions. Reaction 1: a single enantiomer of 2-bromopentane was warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The pentan-2-ol formed was optically active. Reaction 2: a single enantiomer of 3-bromo-3-methylhexane was warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The 3-methylhexan-3-ol formed had no effect on plane-polarised light. Reaction 3: butanal was reacted with HCN in the presence of KCN. The organic product had no effect on plane-polarised light. The table shows initial-rate data for Reactions 1 and 2 at the same temperature. Deduce the rate equation for each reaction. Explain how the rate equations and the optical activity of the products show that Reaction 1 has an SN2 mechanism and Reaction 2 has an SN1 mechanism. You may use diagrams in your answer. Explain why the product of Reaction 3 has no effect on plane-polarised light, although its molecules are chiral. Suggest why optical activity could not be used to find the mechanism of the hydrolysis of 1-bromobutane.
items.ms: Reaction 1: rate = k[2-bromopentane][OH⁻] Reaction 2: rate = k[3-bromo-3-methylhexane] IC1 Reaction 1 is first order in both 2-bromopentane and OH⁻, so both are in the rate-determining step: a one-step SN2 mechanism IC2 the OH⁻ ion attacks the δ+ carbon from the side opposite the C–Br bond as the C–Br bond breaks IC3 through the transition state [HO···C···Br]⁻ the configuration is inverted, so only one enantiomer of pentan-2-ol forms and the product is optically active IC4 Reaction 2 is first order in 3-bromo-3-methylhexane and zero order in OH⁻, so the rate-determining step is the heterolytic breaking of the C–Br bond to form a carbocation (SN1) IC5 the (tertiary) carbocation is planar (trigonal planar around C⁺) IC6 so OH⁻ attacks equally from either side, giving equal amounts of the two enantiomers: a racemic mixture, with no effect on plane-polarised light the C=O group is planar / the carbonyl carbon and the three atoms bonded to it are trigonal planar CN⁻ (the nucleophile) attacks equally from above and below the plane, so equal amounts of the two enantiomers form (a racemic mixture), whose rotations cancel neither 1-bromobutane nor butan-1-ol has a chiral carbon (carbon 1 has two H atoms), so both are optically inactive whichever mechanism occurs
items.why: C15.5 has come up in 11 of 18 sessions (Jan2026, Oct2025, Jan2025); the Jan2023 extended answer on lactic acid showed that a full SN1/SN2 optical-activity argument can fill the 6-mark slot.

items.question: Propanone reacts with hydrogen cyanide in the presence of potassium cyanide. The product is used to make the monomer for the plastic Perspex. CH₃COCH₃ + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN Give the IUPAC name of the product. Draw the mechanism for the reaction of propanone with HCN in the presence of KCN. Include curly arrows, relevant lone pairs and dipoles. Hydrogen cyanide is a weak acid. Ka = 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K. Calculate the concentration of cyanide ions in 0.500 mol dm⁻³ HCN(aq) at 298 K. In the reaction mixture the potassium cyanide gives [CN⁻] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³. Use your answer to (c)(i) to explain why potassium cyanide is added. The table shows the results of experiments to find the rate equation for the reaction at 298 K. Deduce the order of reaction with respect to each of propanone, HCN and CN⁻, and hence write the rate equation. Justify your orders. Calculate the value of the rate constant, k, using the data for Experiment 1. Give its units. Explain how the rate equation is consistent with the mechanism you drew in (b). Suggest why the reaction is very slow if the mixture is made strongly acidic.
items.ms: 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile dipole on the C=O bond (Cδ+, Oδ−) and a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the O atom CN⁻ with a lone pair (and negative charge) on its carbon atom, and a curly arrow from this lone pair to the carbonyl carbon intermediate with a negative charge on the O atom curly arrow from a lone pair on the O⁻ to the H of HCN (and from the H–C bond to the C of CN), giving the product and regenerating CN⁻ [CN⁻]² = Ka × 0.500 or [CN⁻] = √(4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.500) [CN⁻] = 1.57 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ CN⁻ is the nucleophile that attacks the C=O carbon; HCN alone gives a [CN⁻] about 600 times lower, so the reaction would be very slow propanone: first order, because in Experiments 1 and 2 doubling [CH₃COCH₃] doubles the rate HCN: zero order, because in Experiments 2 and 3 doubling [HCN] has no effect on the rate CN⁻: first order, because from Experiment 1 to 4 halving [CH₃COCH₃] alone would halve the rate but the rate rises 1.5 times, so tripling [CN⁻] triples the rate; rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][CN⁻] k = 1.20 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.200 × 0.0100) = 0.0600 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ propanone and CN⁻ (but not HCN) are in the rate equation, so the slow (rate-determining) step is the attack of CN⁻ on the C=O carbon; HCN is used only in the later, fast step H⁺ ions react with CN⁻ to form HCN, so [CN⁻] (the nucleophile) becomes very low
items.why: The HCN mechanism has been drawn in 8 sessions (Oct2024, Jan2024, Oct2023, …); Oct2024 Q18 joined it to the rate equation and the role of base, so a kinetics and Ka link is its likeliest synoptic form.

items.ms: ethanoic acid forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules (it has an H atom bonded to O) methyl methanoate has no H bonded to O, so it has only London forces and permanent dipole forces, which need less energy to overcome propanoic acid has more electrons, so its London forces are stronger both form hydrogen bonds (one COOH group each), so more energy is needed to separate propanoic acid molecules the COOH group of each acid forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules as the hydrocarbon chain gets longer, the non-polar part (which cannot hydrogen bond with water) gets larger / London forces between the acid molecules get stronger, so solubility decreases CH₃(CH₂)₆COOH + NaOH → CH₃(CH₂)₆COONa + H₂O it forms an ionic salt (sodium octanoate / octanoate ions), and the ions are strongly attracted to polar water molecules (ion–dipole attractions / hydrated)

items.ms: phosphorus(V) chloride / PCl₅ hexanoyl chloride Skeletal formula of CH₃(CH₂)₄COCl CH₃(CH₂)₄COCl + H₂O → CH₃(CH₂)₄COOH + HCl A reacts with water (vapour in the air), so it would be hydrolysed to the carboxylic acid (and HCl fumes) ethyl hexanoate CH₃(CH₂)₄CONH₂ as the organic product 2NH₃ on the left and NH₄Cl on the right (balanced) CH₃(CH₂)₄–C(=O)–N(H)–CH₃ with the C=O, C–N, N–H and N–CH₃ bonds shown The HCl formed reacts with a second (basic) methylamine molecule to form methylammonium chloride, CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻ IC1 Direct method: the acid and ethanol are heated under reflux with a (concentrated) sulfuric acid catalyst IC2 CH₃(CH₂)₄COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃(CH₂)₄COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O IC3 The direct reaction is reversible (reaches equilibrium) and slow, so the conversion is incomplete and the yield is lower IC4 With A: A reacts with ethanol at room temperature with no catalyst: CH₃(CH₂)₄COCl + CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃(CH₂)₄COOCH₂CH₃ + HCl IC5 The reaction of A is fast and goes to completion (not reversible), giving a higher yield from A IC6 But the route through A needs an extra step (making A with PCl₅), which lowers the overall yield, and it gives toxic / corrosive HCl (fume cupboard) and needs dry conditions Mr of A = 134.5 and Mr of B = 144 Moles of A = 5.38 ÷ 134.5 = 0.0400, so the maximum mass of B = 0.0400 × 144 = 5.76 g % yield = 4.84 ÷ 5.76 × 100 = 84.0% 8

items.question: Tributyrin is a triester found in butter. Its skeletal formula is shown. When tributyrin is heated under reflux with sodium hydroxide solution, it is hydrolysed to propane-1,2,3-triol and sodium butanoate. Write the equation for the alkaline hydrolysis of tributyrin. Use structural formulae for the organic products. You may use T to represent tributyrin. The purity of a sample of tributyrin is found by a back-titration. • 1.50 g of the sample is heated under reflux with 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution (an excess). • The cooled mixture is made up to 250.0 cm³ with distilled water. • 25.0 cm³ portions are titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. The mean titre is 11.00 cm³. Suggest why the mixture is heated under reflux rather than at room temperature in an open flask. Calculate the percentage by mass of tributyrin in the sample. Use Mr of tributyrin = 302.0 Phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for this titration but methyl orange is not. Explain why. (pH ranges: phenolphthalein 8.2–10.0; methyl orange 3.2–4.4) The sample also contains a little butanoic acid. Explain the effect this has on the calculated percentage of tributyrin. Give two differences between the hydrolysis of tributyrin by dilute hydrochloric acid and its hydrolysis by sodium hydroxide solution. Butanoic acid is obtained from the hydrolysis mixture by adding excess hydrochloric acid. In a trial, a student added only 0.0100 mol of HCl to a solution containing 0.0150 mol of sodium butanoate and no sodium hydroxide. Calculate the pH of the resulting solution. Ka of butanoic acid = 1.51 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ When the hydrolysis mixture is acidified, propane-1,2,3-triol and butanoic acid are obtained. Give the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propane-1,2,3-triol and explain your answer. Give the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of butanoic acid, and the chemical shift range of the peak due to the carbon atom of the COOH group. Use the Data Booklet.
items.ms: Propane-1,2,3-triol: HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH Sodium butanoate: CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa / CH₃CH₂CH₂COO⁻Na⁺ T + 3NaOH → HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH + 3CH₃CH₂CH₂COONa (1 : 3 : 1 : 3 ratio) Hydrolysis is slow at room temperature, so heat is needed to speed it up; reflux stops volatile substances (water / reactants) escaping while the mixture is heated Moles of NaOH added = 0.0250 Moles of HCl in the titre = 0.00110, so moles of NaOH left in 250 cm³ = 0.0110 Moles of NaOH that reacted = 0.0250 − 0.0110 = 0.0140 Moles of tributyrin = 0.0140 ÷ 3 = 0.004667; mass = 0.004667 × 302.0 = 1.409 g Percentage = 1.409 ÷ 1.50 × 100 = 94.0% When the excess NaOH has just been neutralised, the solution contains butanoate ions (a weak base), so the pH at the end point is above 7 (about 8–9), within the range of phenolphthalein Methyl orange changes colour in acidic solution, so the butanoate ions would also react with HCl before the colour change, giving a titre that is too large Butanoic acid also neutralises NaOH, so less NaOH is left (smaller titre) and the calculated percentage of tributyrin is too high Acid hydrolysis is reversible / reaches equilibrium, whereas alkaline hydrolysis goes to completion Acid hydrolysis gives butanoic acid, whereas alkaline hydrolysis gives (sodium) butanoate ions / a salt H⁺ is a catalyst (not used up), whereas OH⁻ is a reactant (3 mol used per mol of tributyrin) Moles of CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH = 0.0100 and moles of CH₃CH₂CH₂COO⁻ left = 0.0050 [H⁺] = Ka × [acid] ÷ [salt] = 1.51 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.0100 ÷ 0.0050 = 3.02 × 10⁻⁵ (mol dm⁻³) pH = 4.52 2, because the two CH₂OH carbon atoms (C1 and C3) are equivalent and the CH(OH) carbon is different 4 (peaks) 160–185 ppm

items.question: 2,2-Dimethylpropanoyl chloride, (CH₃)₃CCOCl, gives one peak in its proton NMR spectrum but three peaks in its ¹³C NMR spectrum. Explain why the two spectra have different numbers of peaks.
items.ms: (Proton NMR) all nine hydrogen atoms are in the same environment / the three CH₃ groups are equivalent, so there is one peak (¹³C NMR) shows every carbon environment, including carbon atoms with no hydrogen atoms: the three CH₃ carbons give one peak, and the central carbon and the C=O carbon are each in a different environment, giving two more peaks
items.why: C15.18 has never been asked on its own; a molecule whose carbon atoms without hydrogens appear only in the ¹³C spectrum tests what ¹³C NMR adds (Jan2020 ER: candidates confuse ¹³C and ¹H NMR).

items.question: How many peaks are there in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of hexanedioic acid, HOOCCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂COOH? 3 4 5 6
items.ms: The molecule is symmetrical: the two COOH carbons are equivalent, C2 and C5 are equivalent, and C3 and C4 are equivalent, so there are three carbon environments. D counts every carbon atom; B and C treat only some of the pairs as equivalent.
items.why: Counting ¹³C peaks for a symmetrical molecule recurs (Jan2026 Q12(a) diol, Oct2024 Q12, May2024 Q13).

items.question: An isomer of C₄H₈O has three peaks in its ¹³C NMR spectrum. One of the peaks is at δ = 204 ppm. Which isomer is it? butanal butanone cyclobutanol 2-methylpropanal
items.ms: 204 ppm is in the range for C=O in aldehydes and ketones (190–220 ppm). 2-methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO, has three carbon environments: CHO, CH and two equivalent CH₃. Butanal (A) and butanone (B) each have four carbon environments; cyclobutanol (C) has three environments but no C=O, so no peak near 200 ppm.
items.why: Using a chemical shift together with the number of peaks (C15.19 i and ii) is the likeliest extension of the peak-count MCQs in Oct2024 Q12 and May2024 Q13.

The spectrum of X has peaks at 177, 60, 34, 19 and 14 ppm. Use the table to identify the type of carbon atom that gives the peak at 177 ppm and the type that gives the peak at 60 ppm. items.ms: 177 ppm: C=O (of an ester) 60 ppm: carbon bonded to oxygen / C–O (the O–CH₂ carbon) Two of the carbon atoms are in the same environment / are equivalent (e.g. two CH₃ groups bonded to the same carbon atom) (CH₃)₂CHCOOH / 2-methylpropanoic acid Three carbon environments: COOH, CH and two equivalent CH₃ groups (butanoic acid would give four peaks) ethyl 2-methylpropanoate (CH₃)₂CHCOOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O ⇌ (CH₃)₂CHCOOH + CH₃CH₂OH 60 ppm and 14 ppm, because they are due to the carbon atoms of the ethyl group (O–CH₂CH₃), which becomes ethanol Ester with a CH₃ group bonded to the C=O (an ethanoate) C(CH₃)₃ group bonded to the ester oxygen: (CH₃)₃COCOCH₃ The carbon atom bonded to the oxygen atom and to three CH₃ groups Each CH₃ group is bonded to a carbon atom with no hydrogen atoms (the C=O carbon and the C bonded to three CH₃ groups), so there are no H atoms on adjacent carbon atoms 3,3-dimethylbutanoic acid, (CH₃)₃CCH₂COOH, or 2-ethylbutanoic acid, (CH₃CH₂)₂CHCOOH
items.why: C15.19 has come up in 15 of 18 sessions; drawing an isomer with a given number of ¹³C peaks was answered correctly by only 20% of candidates (Oct2024 ER), and deducing an ester from its hydrolysis products uses C15.15, which is overdue.

items.name: Proton NMR: low and high resolution; n + 1 rule
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 15 Organic Chemistry Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids

items.question: The high-resolution proton NMR spectrum of a compound has only two peaks: a quartet at δ = 4.3 ppm and a triplet at δ = 1.4 ppm. The relative peak areas are 2 : 3. Which compound gives this spectrum? ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ diethyl ethanedioate, CH₃CH₂OOCCOOCH₂CH₃ ethyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₃ butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃
items.ms: The two ethyl groups of diethyl ethanedioate are equivalent: O–CH₂ (4H, quartet because of the three H atoms on the adjacent CH₃; 4.3 ppm is in the H–C–O range) and CH₃ (6H, triplet because of the adjacent CH₂), so the ratio is 4 : 6 = 2 : 3. A and D also have a singlet from the CH₃ next to C=O, so three peaks; C also has a singlet for the H–C=O proton.
items.why: Matching a high-resolution spectrum to a structure is the commonest C15.20 MCQ (May2024 Q14, Jan2026 Q11(c)); symmetry that reduces the number of peaks is a known trap (Jun2023 ER).

items.name: Proton NMR: low and high resolution; n + 1 rule

items.question: Propyl methanoate is HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃. What is the splitting pattern of the peak due to the CH₂ protons bonded to the oxygen atom in its high-resolution proton NMR spectrum? singlet triplet quartet sextet
items.ms: The O–CH₂ protons have two H atoms on the adjacent carbon atom (the middle CH₂), so n + 1 = 3: a triplet. The H–C=O proton is not on an adjacent carbon atom (an oxygen atom lies between), so it does not split this peak; C counts it. A ignores the neighbouring CH₂; D is the pattern of the middle CH₂, which has five neighbouring H atoms.
items.why: Deducing a splitting pattern with the n + 1 rule was set in Jan2026 Q11(d); an ester oxygen between groups tests which hydrogen atoms count as adjacent.

items.question: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with 2-methylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH, at room temperature to form an ester. Write the equation for this reaction. Use structural formulae. Give the name of the ester. The high-resolution proton NMR spectrum of the ester is shown. Its peaks are at δ = 3.85, 2.05, 1.92 and 0.93 ppm, and the relative peak areas are shown above the peaks. Explain the splitting of the peak at δ = 3.85 ppm and of the peak at δ = 0.93 ppm. Identify the protons that give the singlet at δ = 2.05 ppm and explain why this peak is a singlet. The peak at δ = 1.92 ppm is a multiplet. Use the n + 1 rule to deduce the number of lines in this peak. Give two differences between the high-resolution proton NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropan-1-ol and that of the ester. items.ms: CH₃COCl + (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH → CH₃COOCH₂CH(CH₃)₂ + HCl 2-methylpropyl ethanoate 3.85 ppm: doublet because the O–CH₂ protons are next to a carbon with one hydrogen atom (the CH) 0.93 ppm: doublet because the six protons of the two equivalent CH₃ groups are next to the CH, which has one hydrogen atom The CH₃ group bonded to the C=O / CH₃CO– The adjacent carbon atom (the C=O carbon) has no hydrogen atoms 9 (the CH proton is next to 2 + 3 + 3 = 8 hydrogen atoms) The alcohol has a peak (singlet) of relative area 1 for the O–H proton; the ester has no O–H peak The ester has a singlet of relative area 3 at about 2 ppm (in the H–C–C=O range, from CH₃CO) that the alcohol does not have The O–CH₂ doublet of the alcohol is at a lower chemical shift (about 3.4 ppm) than that of the ester Relative peak areas differ: alcohol 2 : 1 : 1 : 6, ester 2 : 3 : 1 : 6 2-methylpropan-1-ol: 3 ester: 5

items.question: Compound W is a colourless liquid used in fruit flavourings. It contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. The high-resolution mass spectrum of W has a molecular ion peak at m/z = 116.0834. Accurate relative atomic masses: H = 1.0078, C = 12.0000, O = 15.9949 Deduce whether the molecular formula of W is C₆H₁₂O₂, C₇H₁₆O or C₅H₈O₃. Show your working. W is an ester. The table shows the peaks in its high-resolution proton NMR spectrum. Deduce the structure of W. Justify your answer using the chemical shifts, the relative peak areas and the splitting patterns. Proton chemical shift ranges: H–C–O 2.8–4.2 ppm; H–C–C=O 1.6–2.8 ppm; other alkyl protons 0.8–1.8 ppm. The mass spectrum of W has peaks at m/z = 57 and m/z = 43. Give the formula of the ion that causes each peak. Ethyl butanoate is an isomer of W. Explain why the number of peaks in their ¹³C NMR spectra, together with the chemical shift ranges in the Data Booklet, would not distinguish W from ethyl butanoate. Complete the table to predict the chemical shift range and the splitting pattern for three of the proton environments in ethyl butanoate, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₂CH₃. items.ms: C₆H₁₂O₂ = 116.0834; C₇H₁₆O = 116.1197; C₅H₈O₃ = 116.0471 W is C₆H₁₂O₂ IC1 Five peaks, so five proton environments; the areas 2 : 2 : 2 : 3 : 3 account for all 12 H atoms IC2 The peak at 4.03 ppm is in the H–C–O range, so it is a CH₂ bonded to the ester oxygen; it is a triplet, so it is next to a CH₂ IC3 The peak at 2.32 ppm is in the H–C–C=O range, so it is a CH₂ next to the C=O; it is a quartet, so it is next to a CH₃: CH₃CH₂C=O IC4 The sextet at 1.65 ppm is a CH₂ with five hydrogen atoms on adjacent carbons, so it lies between a CH₂ and a CH₃: –OCH₂CH₂CH₃ IC5 The two triplets of area 3 (1.14 and 0.94 ppm) are CH₃ groups each next to a CH₂, at the ends of the ethyl and propyl groups IC6 W is propyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ (not ethyl butanoate, whose O–CH₂ would be a quartet and whose CH₂–C=O would be a triplet) m/z = 57: CH₃CH₂CO⁺ / C₂H₅CO⁺ m/z = 43: CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ / C₃H₇⁺ Both have six carbon atoms in six different environments, so both give six peaks Both have one C=O carbon (160–185 ppm), one C–O carbon (50–90 ppm) and four other alkyl carbons, so the peaks are in the same ranges –O–CH₂–: 2.8–4.2 ppm and quartet –CH₂–C=O: 1.6–2.8 ppm and triplet middle CH₂: 0.8–1.8 ppm and sextet CH₃CH₂COCl + CH₃CH₂CH₂OH → CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ + HCl Moles of acyl chloride = 6.48 ÷ 92.5 = 0.07005 (mol) and Mr of W = 116 Maximum mass of W = 0.07005 × 116 = 8.126 g; % yield = 6.10 ÷ 8.126 × 100 = 75.1%

items.name: Chromatography: mobile and stationary phases
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 15 Organic Chemistry Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids
C15.21 - that chromatography separate
items.question: Chromatography separates the components of a mixture using a mobile phase and a stationary phase. Complete the table to show the mobile phase and the stationary phase in each technique. Explain, in terms of the two phases, why two components of a mixture travel different distances on a TLC plate.
items.ms: TLC: mobile phase = (liquid) solvent; stationary phase = silica / alumina (thin layer on the plate) GC: mobile phase = (inert) carrier gas, e.g. nitrogen, helium or argon; stationary phase = (non-volatile) liquid (on a solid support) in the column The components have different relative attractions to (or solubilities in) the stationary phase and the mobile phase, so the one more strongly attracted to the stationary phase (or less soluble in the solvent) travels a shorter distance
items.why: C15.21 is a cool point asked only as MCQs (Oct2023 Q13(b), Jan2021 Q16); naming both phases for TLC and GC is the most direct test of it.

items.name: Rf values from one-way chromatograms
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 15 Organic Chemistry Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids

items.question: A mixture of two compounds, P and Q, is separated by thin-layer chromatography. The solvent front moves 7.6 cm from the start line. The Rf value of P is 0.45 and the Rf value of Q is 0.70. What is the distance between the centres of the spots of P and Q? 1.9 cm 3.4 cm 5.3 cm 8.7 cm
items.ms: Distance moved = Rf × distance moved by the solvent front: P = 0.45 × 7.6 = 3.42 cm and Q = 0.7 × 7.6 = 5.32 cm, so the spots are 1.9 cm apart. B and C are the distances of P and of Q from the start line; D adds the two distances.
items.why: Rf calculations (C15.22) are set as an MCQ in most sessions (Oct2025 Q10(c), Jun2025 Q8, Jan2023 Q16); this one uses Rf in reverse for two spots.

items.name: Rf values from one-way chromatograms
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: A student makes ethyl butanoate by heating butanoic acid with ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid. After 30 minutes, the student spots the reaction mixture (M), pure butanoic acid (A) and pure ethyl butanoate (E) on the start line of a silica TLC plate. The plate is developed in a solvent that is mostly hexane. The diagram shows the plate after development. Calculate the Rf value of ethyl butanoate. The student concludes that all the butanoic acid has reacted. Comment on this conclusion. Use the chromatogram. The plate is run again using a solvent that contains a greater proportion of a more polar liquid. Explain the effect on the Rf value of butanoic acid.
items.ms: Rf = 4.5 ÷ 6.0 = 0.75 The conclusion is wrong: M has a spot at the same height / same Rf (0.30) as butanoic acid, so unreacted butanoic acid is still present The Rf value (of butanoic acid) increases / the spot moves further (Butanoic acid is polar, so) it is more strongly attracted to / more soluble in the more polar mobile phase compared with the (polar silica) stationary phase
items.why: Rf calculations (C15.22) were asked in Oct2025, Jun2025 and Jan2023; the spec's 'reasons for differences in Rf values' has been asked only once (Jan2020 Q16(b)(ii)).

items.name: HPLC and GC: retention times, links to mass spectrometry
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 15 Organic Chemistry Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids

items.question: A urine sample from an athlete is analysed by gas chromatography linked to a mass spectrometer (GC–MS). Which statement is correct? The retention time alone identifies each compound with certainty. The components are separated in the mass spectrometer and then detected in the column. The mass spectrum of each separated component is compared with spectra in a database to identify it. The carrier gas reacts with each component so that it can be detected.
items.ms: GC separates the components (they have different retention times); each then passes into the mass spectrometer, and its mass spectrum (molecular ion and fragmentation pattern) is matched with a database. A: different compounds can have the same retention time. B reverses the roles of the column and the mass spectrometer. D: the carrier gas is inert and does not react.
items.why: The spec names drug testing in sport for GC–MS (C15.23), but recent MCQs (Oct2025 Q10, Oct2022 Q14) asked only about the GC stage.

items.name: HPLC and GC: retention times, links to mass spectrometry
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 15 Organic Chemistry Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids
C15.23 - that high-performance liquid
items.question: Gas chromatography (GC) is used to test athletes' urine for a banned stimulant, X. Substances are extracted from the urine and the extract is injected into a gas chromatograph. The chromatogram of an extract is shown. A pure sample of X has a retention time of 6.4 minutes under the same conditions. Identify the peak in the chromatogram that could be due to X. Explain why the substances in the extract have different retention times. Before a positive result is reported, the extract is analysed by GC linked to a mass spectrometer (GC–MS). Explain why. The concentration of X is found from its peak area, which is proportional to the amount of X. • 5.00 cm³ of urine was extracted and the extract was made up to 10.0 cm³ of solution. • A standard solution of X with a concentration of 4.00 μg cm⁻³ gave a peak area of 1.60 × 10⁴ (arbitrary units). • The solution made from the urine gave a peak area for X of 2.70 × 10⁴. The limit for X is 10.0 μg cm⁻³ in urine. Deduce whether the concentration of X in the athlete's urine is above this limit. Show your working.
items.ms: R The substances have different attractions to / solubilities in the (liquid) stationary phase compared with the (carrier gas) mobile phase A substance that is more strongly attracted to the stationary phase moves through the column more slowly, so it has a longer retention time A different compound could have the same retention time as X, so GC alone does not identify X with certainty The mass spectrometer gives the molecular ion peak / fragmentation pattern of the substance with that retention time, which is compared with that of X / a database Concentration of X in the solution = 4.00 × (2.70 × 10⁴ ÷ 1.60 × 10⁴) = 6.75 μg cm⁻³ Concentration in the urine = 6.75 × (10.0 ÷ 5.00) = 13.5 μg cm⁻³ 13.5 μg cm⁻³ is greater than 10.0 μg cm⁻³, so the limit is exceeded
items.why: C15.23 was asked in 9 of 18 sessions; the spec names drug testing in sport, and a peak-area calculation (like Jan2025 Q20(e)(ii)) is the least-asked quantitative angle.

items.name: Enthalpy alone does not decide feasibility
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 12 Entropy and Energetics
C12.1 - that, since endothermic reactions can occur s
items.question: A student adds 5.0 g of solid ammonium carbonate to 50 cm³ of aqueous ethanoic acid in a polystyrene cup. The mixture fizzes and the temperature falls from 21.0 °C to 14.5 °C. (NH₄)₂CO₃(s) + 2CH₃COOH(aq) → 2CH₃COONH₄(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) The student's notes say: 'Only exothermic reactions can take place by themselves at room temperature.' Explain how the observations show that this statement is incorrect. Explain, in terms of entropy changes, why this reaction is feasible at room temperature.
items.ms: The temperature falls, so the reaction is endothermic / ΔrH is positive, yet it takes place by itself (spontaneously) at room temperature ΔSsurroundings is negative (because ΔrH is positive / heat energy is taken in from the surroundings) ΔSsystem is positive because a gas is produced / the number of moles increases from 3 to 4 ΔSsystem is larger than the magnitude of ΔSsurroundings, so ΔStotal is positive
items.why: Endothermic reactions that happen by themselves were asked in Jun2021 Q15 and Jan2025 Q19; the ammonium carbonate and ethanoic acid reaction is a suggested practical that has not been used.

items.name: Entropy as disorder; dispersal of molecules and energy quanta
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 12 Entropy and Energetics
C12.2 - entropy as a measure of diso
items.question: Poly(ethene) is made by polymerising ethene gas at high pressure. n C₂H₄(g) → (C₂H₄)ₙ(s) Explain, in terms of the dispersal of molecules and of energy quanta, why the entropy of the system decreases during this polymerisation.
items.ms: n gas molecules join to form one molecule in a solid, so the particles are less dispersed / more ordered / there are fewer ways of arranging them there are fewer (independent) molecules, so there are fewer ways of distributing the energy quanta (between the molecules)
items.why: C12.2's disorder and energy-quanta wording was rewarded in Oct2020 Q19(a)(ii) and Jun2024 Q15(a)(ii); a polymerisation, with a very large fall in the number of molecules, has not been used.

items.name: Entropy rises with temperature and solid → liquid → gas; zero at 0 K for a perfect crystal
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 12 Entropy and Energetics
C12.3 - that the entropy of a substa
items.question: Which statement about entropy is correct? A perfect crystal at 0 K has zero entropy. The standard molar entropy of an element in its standard state is zero. The entropy of a substance stays constant as it is heated, until it changes state. One mole of steam at 373 K has the same entropy as one mole of liquid water at 373 K.
items.ms: A is correct: the particles of a perfect crystal at 0 K are perfectly ordered and have no energy quanta to distribute, so there is only one possible arrangement. B confuses entropy with ΔfH°: elements have positive standard molar entropies (e.g. O₂(g) 205.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). C is wrong because entropy increases with temperature (more energy quanta, more ways of distributing them). D is wrong because the gas is far more disordered than the liquid, so entropy rises on boiling.
items.why: C12.3 has come up in 11 of 18 sessions, mostly as 'greatest standard molar entropy' MCQs; zero entropy for a perfect crystal and the non-zero entropy of elements have not been tested.

items.name: Entropy rises with temperature and solid → liquid → gas; zero at 0 K for a perfect crystal
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 12 Entropy and Energetics
C12.3 - that the entropy of a substa
items.question: At a pressure of 100 kPa, solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) does not melt. It sublimes at 195 K. Assume that solid carbon dioxide forms a perfect crystal. Sketch, on the axes, how the entropy of one mole of carbon dioxide changes as it is heated from 0 K to 300 K at 100 kPa. Explain why the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at 0 K.
items.ms: Line starts at the origin (zero entropy at 0 K) Entropy increases with temperature both below and above 195 K One vertical increase only, at 195 K The particles are perfectly ordered and have no (thermal) energy to distribute, so there is only one way of arranging the particles and their energy
items.why: The entropy–temperature sketch was asked in Jun2021 Q20(c) and Oct2025 Q19(d), both for water; a substance that sublimes (one vertical step) and zero entropy at 0 K have not been tested.

items.name: Direction of change is increasing total entropy; gases spread spontaneously
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 12 Entropy and Energetics

items.question: An air freshener is sprayed into one corner of a closed room in which the air is still. A few minutes later it can be smelled in every part of the room. The vapour never collects back in the corner where it was sprayed. Explain these observations in terms of entropy.
items.ms: The vapour molecules move randomly and spread through the whole volume, so there are more ways of arranging the molecules (and their energy) / the entropy of the system increases Changes take place naturally in the direction of increasing total entropy / ΔStotal is positive Collecting back in the corner would decrease the entropy / give a negative ΔStotal, so it does not happen by itself

items.name: Entropy changes in changes of state, dissolving a lattice, and changes in moles
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: For which change is ΔSsystem negative? CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) KNO₃(s) → K⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) Br₂(l) → Br₂(g) Ca(OH)₂(s) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l)
items.ms: D: the number of moles does not change (2 → 2), but the only gas is used up to form a solid and a liquid, so the disorder decreases (ΔSsystem ≈ −134 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). A forms a gas from a solid; B breaks up an ordered lattice into ions that move freely in solution; C changes a liquid into a gas. A, B and C all have a positive ΔSsystem.
items.why: C12.5 appears in 11 of 18 sessions (Jan2026 Q3 and Jan2020 Q7 asked for the largest increase); a change with the same number of moles on each side but a gas used up has not been an option.

items.question: This question is about the entropy changes of some processes. The table shows some standard molar entropies at 298 K. Hydrogen burns in a car engine, forming steam. 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g) Without doing a calculation, explain why ΔSsystem for this reaction is negative. In a fuel cell at 298 K, the water forms as a liquid. 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) Calculate ΔSsystem for this reaction. Include a sign and units in your answer. ΔSsystem for the reaction forming steam in (a) is −88.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Explain why your answer to (b)(i) is much more negative. The table shows ΔSsystem for two dissolving processes at 298 K. Explain why ΔSsystem is positive when solid potassium nitrate dissolves, but negative when hydrogen chloride gas dissolves, even though both processes form two moles of ions from one mole of substance.
items.ms: 3 mol of gas form 2 mol of gas / the number of gas molecules decreases so there are fewer ways of arranging the molecules / of distributing the energy (quanta), so there is less disorder ΔSsystem = (2 × 69.9) − (2 × 130.6 + 205.0) = −326.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ In (b)(i) all of the gas becomes liquid (3 mol of gas → no gas) and a liquid has much lower entropy than a gas / is much more ordered than a gas (KNO₃) the ions are held in fixed positions in the ordered lattice but move randomly in solution, so the disorder increases (HCl) gas molecules are very disordered / move freely through the whole container, but the ions are confined to the solution / are much less free to move (HCl) the decrease in entropy when the gas dissolves outweighs the increase from forming two particles from one water molecules become ordered around the ions (hydration), which lowers the entropy
items.why: C12.5 appears in 11 of 18 sessions, usually as counting moles of gas; the effect of the state of a product (H₂O(l) against H₂O(g)) and a lattice dissolving compared with a gas dissolving have not been asked.

items.question: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly at room temperature. 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) At 298 K, ΔStotal = +783 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and ΔSsurroundings = +0.658 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔSsystem for this reaction at 298 K. Include a sign and units in your answer.
items.ms: ΔSsystem = ΔStotal − ΔSsurroundings with both in the same units, e.g. 783 − 658 = +125 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.why: ΔS_{total} = ΔS_{system} + ΔS_{surroundings} underlies the calculations in 6 sessions, but working back to ΔS_{system} (Oct2020 Q19(a)(iv)) is rare, and mixing kJ and J is the error the examiner reports name most.

path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Ammonia is oxidised in the first stage of the manufacture of nitric acid. 4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(g) The table shows some standard molar entropies. What is ΔSsystem, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, for this reaction? −180.8 +2.1 +180.8 +1000.8
items.ms: C: ΔSsystem = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants) = (4 × 210.7 + 6 × 188.7) − (4 × 192.3 + 5 × 205.0) = +180.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. A subtracts products from reactants; B ignores the coefficients; D multiplies every entropy except that of oxygen.
items.why: ΔS_{system} MCQ calculations appeared in Jun2021, Jan2024 and Jan2026; the examiner reports say the commonest error is not multiplying by the coefficients.
