items.question: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔSsystem = −187.8 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. S°[SO₂(g)] = 248.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and S°[O₂(g)] = 205.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is the standard molar entropy of SO₃(g), in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹? 154.2 256.7 444.5 513.4
items.ms: B: 2S°[SO₃] = ΔSsystem + 2S°[SO₂] + S°[O₂] = −187.8 + 496.2 + 205.0 = 513.4, so S°[SO₃] = 256.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. A leaves out oxygen; C uses +187.8 for ΔSsystem; D does not divide by 2.
items.why: Working back to a standard molar entropy from ΔS_{system} was asked in Jan2022 Q22(a) as a structured part; it has not yet been an MCQ.

items.question: Ethanol is manufactured by the direct hydration of ethene, as shown in the diagram. C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g) The table shows some data at 298 K. Suggest why the standard molar entropy of ethanol gas is greater than that of ethene gas. Calculate ΔSsystem for the reaction. Include a sign and units in your answer. When the gases leaving the reactor are cooled, the ethanol condenses. For the reaction C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(l) ΔSsystem = −247.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Calculate the standard molar entropy of liquid ethanol, C₂H₅OH(l). Explain why your answer to (c)(i) is less than the standard molar entropy of ethanol gas. The reactor operates at 573 K. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔrH, for the reaction C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g). Calculate ΔSsurroundings and ΔStotal at 573 K. Include signs and units in your answers. Assume that ΔrH and ΔSsystem do not change with temperature. Calculate the highest temperature at which the reaction is feasible. Use the same assumption as in (d)(ii). Suggest why the reactor is operated at 573 K and 60 atm. Refer to your answers to (d)(ii) and (e).
items.ms: Ethanol molecules have more atoms / are larger / more complex, so there are more ways of distributing the energy (quanta) ΔSsystem = 282.7 − (219.5 + 188.7) = −125.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ S°[C₂H₅OH(l)] = −247.5 + (219.5 + 188.7) = 160.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Molecules in a liquid are closer together / less free to move than in a gas, so there are fewer ways of arranging them (and their energy) / the liquid is more ordered ΔrH = −235.1 − (+52.3 + (−241.8)) = −45.6 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔSsurroundings = −(−45600) ÷ 573 = +79.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal = −125.5 + 79.6 = −45.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ T = ΔrH ÷ ΔSsystem (when ΔStotal = 0) = 45600 ÷ 125.5 = 363 K At 363 K or below the rate would be too slow (even with the catalyst) ΔStotal is only slightly negative, so the equilibrium constant is small but not zero / some ethanol still forms The high pressure (60 atm, not 1 atm) moves the position of equilibrium to the right (fewer moles of gas), increasing the yield Unreacted ethene is recycled, so the overall conversion is high
items.why: ΔS_{system} calculations appear in 15 of 18 sessions; working back to a standard molar entropy has been asked only once (Jan2022 Q22(a)), and a process run where ΔS_{total} is negative has not been asked.

items.question: The enthalpy change of combustion of methane is −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ at 25 °C. What is the entropy change of the surroundings, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, at this temperature? −2988 +2.988 +2988 +35 600

items.question: Dinitrogen tetroxide, N₂O₄, is a colourless gas. It decomposes to form brown nitrogen dioxide, NO₂. N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) A student measured the equilibrium constant, Kp, at different temperatures and used the relationship ΔStotal = R ln Kp to calculate ΔStotal at each temperature. The results are shown in the table. Write the expression for Kp for this equilibrium and give its units. Explain, without doing a calculation, why ΔSsystem for the forward reaction is positive. Use the expressions ΔStotal = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurroundings and ΔSsurroundings = −ΔH ÷ T to explain why a graph of ΔStotal against 1/T is a straight line, and state what its gradient represents. Assume that ΔH and ΔSsystem do not change with temperature. Use the data in the table. Complete the table by calculating the two missing values of 1/T. Plot a graph of ΔStotal (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis) on the grid and draw a line of best fit. Determine the gradient of your line and hence the value of ΔH, in kJ mol⁻¹, for the forward reaction. Use your graph to find the temperature at which ΔStotal = 0. Hence calculate ΔSsystem for the forward reaction. Explain why ΔStotal for this reaction increases as the temperature increases. A sealed glass tube containing an equilibrium mixture of N₂O₄ and NO₂ is moved from iced water at 273 K into hot water at 353 K. Use the relationship ΔStotal = R ln Kp to explain the colour change that is seen.
items.ms: Kp = p(NO₂)² ÷ p(N₂O₄) atm 1 mol of gas forms 2 mol of gas, so there are more ways of arranging the molecules / of distributing the energy quanta ΔStotal = −ΔH × (1/T) + ΔSsystem, which has the form y = mx + c (−ΔH and ΔSsystem are constants) The gradient is −ΔH (in J mol⁻¹) 3.14 (318 K) and 2.96 (338 K) Axes labelled with quantities and units, and scales chosen so that the points cover at least half of the grid in each direction All six points plotted correctly (to within half a small square) Straight line of best fit Gradient = Δy ÷ Δx using two points on the line that are far apart, with 1/T in K⁻¹ (not 10⁻³ K⁻¹) Gradient = −5.6 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ ΔH = −gradient = +56 kJ mol⁻¹ 1/T read from the graph where ΔStotal = 0: 3.07 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹ T = 1 ÷ (3.07 × 10⁻³) = 325 K ΔSsystem = ΔH ÷ T = 56 000 ÷ 325 = +172 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ The forward reaction is endothermic, so ΔSsurroundings is negative As T increases, −ΔH ÷ T becomes less negative / the magnitude of ΔSsurroundings decreases ΔSsystem (positive) does not change significantly, so ΔStotal increases / becomes positive above about 325 K ΔStotal becomes more positive (it changes from negative to positive), so ln Kp and Kp increase The position of equilibrium moves to the right / more NO₂ forms, so the mixture becomes darker brown
items.why: C12.8 has come up in 16 of 18 sessions; the ΔS_{total} against 1/T graph, a 'beyond spec but examined' item, was set only in Jan2022 and is due to return in a new context.

items.question: For the reaction 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔrH = −114.2 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔSsystem = −146.4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Assume that these values do not change with temperature. Which statement is correct? The reaction is feasible only below 780 K. The reaction is feasible only above 780 K. The reaction is feasible at all temperatures. The reaction is not feasible at any temperature.
items.ms: A: ΔSsurroundings = +114 200 ÷ T is positive but gets smaller as T rises, while ΔSsystem stays at −146.4; ΔStotal = 0 when T = 114 200 ÷ 146.4 = 780 K, so ΔStotal is positive only below 780 K. B reverses the effect of temperature; C would need a positive ΔSsystem; D would need an endothermic reaction with a negative ΔSsystem.
items.why: Feasibility from the signs of ΔH and ΔS_{system} was asked in Jan2025 Q9, Oct2024 Q11 and Jan2026 Q17; the upper temperature limit of an exothermic reaction with a negative ΔS_{system} is the less-asked case.

items.question: Sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, is used as a raising agent in baking. When it is heated it decomposes. 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(g) The table shows some thermodynamic data at 298 K. Explain, without doing a calculation, why ΔSsystem for this reaction is positive. Use the data in the table. Calculate the enthalpy change of reaction, ΔrH. Calculate ΔSsystem. Include a sign and units in your answer. Calculate ΔStotal for the reaction at 298 K. Use your answer to explain why sodium hydrogencarbonate does not decompose at room temperature. Calculate the lowest temperature, in °C, at which the decomposition is feasible. Assume that ΔrH and ΔSsystem do not change with temperature. A sample of sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated to 433 K in a sealed steel container from which the air has been removed. An equilibrium is set up. 2NaHCO₃(s) ⇌ Na₂CO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(g) The diagram shows the apparatus. Write the expression for Kp for this equilibrium. Calculate ΔStotal at 433 K and hence the value of Kp at this temperature. Give the units of Kp. Use ΔStotal = R ln Kp, where R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate the total pressure in the container at equilibrium at 433 K. When a cake is baked in an open oven at 433 K, all of the sodium hydrogencarbonate decomposes. Explain why, even though Kp is not very large. Explain, in terms of entropy changes, how the value of Kp changes if the sealed container is heated to 473 K instead of 433 K.
items.ms: 2 mol of solid form 1 mol of solid and 2 mol of gas / gases are produced from a solid ΔrH = (−1130.7 + (−393.5) + (−241.8)) − 2 × (−950.8) = +135.6 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔSsystem = (135.0 + 213.6 + 188.7) − 2 × 101.7 = +333.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔSsurroundings = −(+135600) ÷ 298 = −455.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal = +333.9 + (−455.0) = −121.1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal is negative, so the decomposition is not feasible at 298 K T = ΔrH ÷ ΔSsystem = 135600 ÷ 333.9 = 406 K = 133 °C Kp = p(CO₂) × p(H₂O) ΔStotal = 333.9 − (135600 ÷ 433) = +20.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ln Kp = 20.7 ÷ 8.31 = 2.49 Kp = 12.1 atm² p(CO₂) = p(H₂O), so p(CO₂) = √Kp = √12.1 = 3.48 atm Total pressure = 2 × 3.48 = 6.96 atm The carbon dioxide and steam escape, so equilibrium is never reached / p(CO₂) × p(H₂O) stays below Kp so the forward reaction continues / the position keeps moving to the right until all the NaHCO₃ has decomposed ΔSsurroundings (= −ΔrH ÷ T) becomes less negative while ΔSsystem stays the same, so ΔStotal becomes more positive so ln Kp and Kp increase
items.why: Feasibility-temperature calculations appear in 14 of 18 sessions (most recently Oct2025 Q9(d)); linking ΔS_{total} to K_{p} for a heterogeneous decomposition and the gas pressure it produces has not been set.

items.question: The thermite reaction is used to weld railway lines. A mixture of powdered aluminium and iron(III) oxide is lit with burning magnesium ribbon, as shown in the diagram. Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s) The table shows some data at 298 K. Calculate ΔSsystem for the reaction. Include a sign and units in your answer. Use the data in the table. Calculate ΔSsurroundings at 298 K. Calculate ΔStotal at 298 K. A thermite mixture can be stored for years without reacting. Once it is lit with burning magnesium, it reacts vigorously and produces molten iron at about 2800 K. Discuss these observations in terms of the entropy changes and the activation energy of the reaction. Use your answers to (a) and (b).
items.ms: ΔSsystem = (50.9 + 2 × 27.3) − (87.4 + 2 × 28.3) = −38.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔrH = −1675.7 − (−824.2) = −851.5 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔSsurroundings = −(−851500) ÷ 298 = +2857 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal = −38.5 + 2857 = +2819 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ IC1 ΔSsystem is negative (−38.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and small, because all the substances are solids and the number of moles does not change IC2 The reaction is very exothermic, so ΔSsurroundings is large and positive and ΔStotal is positive: the reaction is feasible / thermodynamically unstable even though ΔSsystem is negative IC3 The mixture does not react at room temperature because the activation energy is very high / the mixture is kinetically stable / very few particles have energy ≥ Ea IC4 The burning magnesium supplies (heat) energy so that particles have enough energy to overcome the activation energy IC5 The energy released heats the rest of the mixture so that it also reacts / the reaction keeps itself going and the rate increases as the temperature rises IC6 At 2800 K, ΔSsurroundings is smaller (+304 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) but still much larger than the magnitude of ΔSsystem, so ΔStotal is still positive and the reaction remains feasible
items.why: C12.10 is tested only inside ΔS_{total} calculations (Jan2020 Q19, Jan2023 Q20); the Jun2023 examiner report criticised answers that judged ΔS_{total} without the activation energy, so a 6-mark answer combining both is a likely new angle.

items.name: Thermodynamic against kinetic stability
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 12 Entropy and Energetics
C12.11 - and distinguish between the
items.question: Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon. C(diamond) → C(graphite) ΔH = −1.9 kJ mol⁻¹ At 298 K, ΔSsystem = +3.3 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and ΔStotal = +9.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The reaction profile for this change is shown (not to scale). Explain what the value of ΔStotal shows about the thermodynamic stability of diamond at 298 K. Diamonds do not change into graphite, even over millions of years at room temperature. Use the reaction profile to explain why.
items.ms: ΔStotal is positive, so the change into graphite is (thermodynamically) feasible / diamond is thermodynamically unstable relative to graphite The activation energy is (very) high because many strong covalent (C–C) bonds in the giant lattice must be broken so at room temperature (almost) no atoms have energy ≥ Ea; the rate is negligible / diamond is kinetically stable (so diamond changes into graphite only when it is heated to a very high temperature)
items.why: C12.11 is cool (3 of 18 sessions, last Jun2024); the mark schemes reward 'feasible because ΔS_{total} is positive' plus 'strong bonds, high activation energy, so the rate is very slow' (Jun2023 Q20(c), Jun2024 Q15(a)(v), a giant covalent SiO₂ reaction); diamond, the textbook case of a feasible change that never happens, has not been used.

items.question: Which equation represents the lattice energy of calcium fluoride? CaF₂(s) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2F⁻(g) Ca(s) + F₂(g) → CaF₂(s) Ca²⁺(aq) + 2F⁻(aq) → CaF₂(s) Ca²⁺(g) + 2F⁻(g) → CaF₂(s)

items.ms: X: Ca²⁺(g) + 2Cl(g) + 2e⁻ Y: Ca⁺(g) + Cl₂(g) + e⁻ A: (twice the standard) enthalpy change of atomisation of chlorine B: (twice the first) electron affinity of chlorine lattice energy = −795.8 − (178.2 + 590 + 1145 + 243.4 − 697.6) / = −795.8 − (1459.0) = −2255 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔfH = 178.2 + 590 + 121.7 + (−348.8) + (−719) = −177.9 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔH = ΔfH(CaCl₂) − 2 × ΔfH(CaCl) = −795.8 − 2(−177.9) = −440.0 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔSsurroundings = −ΔH/T = +440000 ÷ 298 = +1477 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, large and positive, while ΔSsystem is small because all the substances are solids so ΔStotal is positive: the change of CaCl into Ca and CaCl₂ is feasible / CaCl is thermodynamically unstable with respect to Ca and CaCl₂

items.question: The theoretical lattice energy of an ionic compound is calculated using electrostatic theory. Which is not an assumption made in this calculation? The ions are perfect spheres. The ions are in contact with each other in the lattice. The electron cloud of the anion is distorted by the cation. The bonding is 100% ionic.
items.ms: C: the model treats the ions as undistorted spheres (point charges); distortion (polarisation) of the anion is exactly what the model leaves out, and it is why the Born–Haber value can be more exothermic. A, B and D are all assumptions of the purely ionic model.

items.question: Lithium–iodine cells are used in heart pacemakers because they last for many years. The overall reaction in the cell is 2Li(s) + I₂(s) → 2LiI(s) The standard enthalpy change of formation of lithium iodide, LiI(s), is −270.4 kJ mol⁻¹. Some standard entropies are given in the table. Calculate ΔStotal for the cell reaction at body temperature, 37 °C, and deduce whether the reaction is thermodynamically feasible. The table gives some more enthalpy changes. Use these data and the enthalpy change of formation in (a) to calculate the lattice energy of lithium iodide. items.ms: ΔSsystem = 2(86.8) − [2(29.1) + 116.1] = −0.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔSsurroundings = −(2 × −270.4 × 1000) ÷ 310 = +1745 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal = +1744 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; positive, so the reaction is feasible lattice energy = −270.4 − (159.4 + 520 + 106.8 − 295.4) = −761 kJ mol⁻¹ the bonding is 100% ionic / there is no covalent character the ions are perfect spheres / point charges / are not distorted (polarised) the ions are in contact / the distance between the ions is the sum of the ionic radii (761 − 730) ÷ 730 × 100 = 4.2 (%) IC1 KF (and LiF): the experimental value is (almost) the same as the theoretical value, so the bonding is (almost) 100% ionic / the ionic model fits IC2 an experimental value more exothermic than the theoretical value shows covalent character; the larger the percentage difference, the greater the covalent character IC3 covalent character arises because the cation polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the anion, so there is some electron density between the ions IC4 Li⁺ is smaller than K⁺ (same charge), so it has a higher charge density / greater polarising power: LiF > KF and LiI > KI IC5 I⁻ is larger than F⁻, so its electron cloud is more easily polarised (more polarisable): LiI > LiF and KI > KF IC6 LiI has the greatest covalent character (smallest cation with largest anion) and KF the least; order KF < LiF < KI < LiI Li⁺ is smaller than K⁺ F⁻ is smaller than I⁻ so the ions in LiF are closest together (smallest sum of ionic radii), giving the strongest electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions (the charges are the same in all three) ΔsolH = (−519) + (−293) − (−761) = −51 kJ mol⁻¹

items.name: Polarisation of anions by cations
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 12 Entropy and Energetics

items.question: Which statement about polarisation in ionic compounds is correct? A cation with a large radius and a small charge has a high polarising power. An anion with a large radius and a large charge is easily polarised. Polarisation of the anion makes the Born–Haber lattice energy less exothermic than the theoretical value. Covalent character arises mainly because the anion polarises the cation.
items.ms: B: a large anion with a high charge holds its outer electrons less tightly, so its electron cloud is easily distorted (high polarisability). A: high polarising power needs a small, highly charged cation (high charge density). C: polarisation adds covalent character, so the Born–Haber value is more exothermic than the theoretical value. D: it is the cation that polarises the anion.
items.why: C12.15 is hot (14 of 18 sessions) and the examiner reports list confusing polarising power with polarisability, and the direction of the lattice-energy difference, as common errors (Jun2023, Jan2024).

items.question: Aluminium fluoride, AlF₃, is a high-melting solid whose bonding is mainly ionic. Aluminium iodide, AlI₃, melts at 189 °C and its bonding has considerable covalent character. The table gives the radii of the ions. Explain, in terms of polarisation, why the bonding in aluminium iodide has much more covalent character than the bonding in aluminium fluoride.
items.ms: Al³⁺ is small and highly charged, so it has a high charge density / high polarising power I⁻ is larger than F⁻, so its outer electrons are further from the nucleus / its electron cloud is more easily distorted (more polarisable) Al³⁺ distorts the electron cloud of I⁻ so that electron density is drawn into the region between the ions, giving (partial) sharing of electrons / covalent character F⁻ is small and is not easily polarised, so AlF₃ stays mainly ionic

items.question: Which equation represents the enthalpy change of hydration of the sulfate ion? SO₄²⁻(aq) → SO₄²⁻(g) SO₄²⁻(g) + aq → SO₄²⁻(aq) Na₂SO₄(s) + aq → 2Na⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) SO₄²⁻(g) + H₂O(l) → HSO₄⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

items.question: The energy level diagram for dissolving potassium nitrate, KNO₃, in water is shown. P, Q and R are the enthalpy changes in the directions of the arrows. Which expression, in terms of P and Q, gives the enthalpy change of solution of potassium nitrate? P + Q P − Q −P − Q Q − P
items.ms: D: R is the enthalpy change of solution; by Hess's law P + R = Q, so R = Q − P (the sum of the hydration enthalpies minus the lattice energy). A adds the lattice energy instead of subtracting it; B has the signs reversed (it equals −R); C treats both changes as if they were endothermic.
items.why: The spec names energy level diagrams for Δ_{sol}H, but MCQs have used only cycles and data (Jan2025 asked for a sketched diagram in a 3-mark part); reading an endothermic dissolving diagram is a likely new MCQ.

items.question: Silver fluoride, AgF, is very soluble in water, but silver chloride, AgCl, is almost insoluble. When aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution of chloride ions a white precipitate forms, but no precipitate forms with a solution of fluoride ions. A student dissolved 3.81 g of silver fluoride in 50.0 g of water in an insulated cup. The temperature rose from 20.4 °C to 23.6 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of silver fluoride. Use only the mass of the water, and its specific heat capacity, 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. [M(AgF) = 126.9 g mol⁻¹] The Hess cycle relates the enthalpy change of solution of silver fluoride to its lattice energy and the enthalpy changes of hydration of its ions. Complete the Hess cycle by writing the formulae, including state symbols, of the species in the box and labelling the two arrows with the enthalpy changes they represent. The enthalpy changes of hydration of Ag⁺ and F⁻ are −464 kJ mol⁻¹ and −506 kJ mol⁻¹. Use these values and your answer to (a) to calculate the lattice energy of silver fluoride. The experimental lattice energy of silver chloride is −893 kJ mol⁻¹ and the enthalpy change of hydration of Cl⁻ is −364 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of silver chloride. The theoretical lattice energies of silver fluoride and silver chloride, calculated assuming purely ionic bonding, are −920 kJ mol⁻¹ and −833 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain why the experimental lattice energy of silver chloride differs from its theoretical value by much more than that of silver fluoride does. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution that silver chloride would have if its bonding were purely ionic. Use your answer to explain how the covalent character of silver chloride affects its solubility. Silver chloride dissolves in water to a very small extent. AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) The table gives some standard entropies at 298 K. Calculate ΔSsystem for dissolving silver chloride. Use your answers to (c) and (e)(i) to calculate ΔStotal for dissolving silver chloride at 298 K. Write the expression for the equilibrium constant, Kc, for this equilibrium. Use the relationship ΔStotal = R ln K and your answer to (e)(ii) to calculate the value of Kc at 298 K. Hence calculate the solubility of silver chloride, in mol dm⁻³. [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹] For dissolving silver fluoride at 298 K, ΔStotal = +50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Use the values of ΔStotal to explain the observations with aqueous silver nitrate described at the start of the question.
items.ms: energy transferred = 50.0 × 4.18 × 3.2 = 668.8 J n(AgF) = 3.81 ÷ 126.9 = 0.03002 mol ΔsolH = −668.8 ÷ (0.03002 × 1000) = −22.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (negative sign needed) Ag⁺(g) + F⁻(g) in the box left arrow: lattice energy (of AgF) AND right arrow: ΔhydH(Ag⁺) + ΔhydH(F⁻) / enthalpy changes of hydration of the ions lattice energy = ΔhydH(Ag⁺) + ΔhydH(F⁻) − ΔsolH = (−464) + (−506) − (−22.3) = −948 kJ mol⁻¹ ΔsolH = (−464) + (−364) − (−893) = +65 kJ mol⁻¹ Cl⁻ is larger than F⁻ so the electron cloud of Cl⁻ is more easily distorted (polarised) by Ag⁺ so AgCl has more covalent character, and the extra attraction makes its experimental lattice energy more exothermic than the purely ionic (theoretical) value ΔsolH = (−464) + (−364) − (−833) = +5 kJ mol⁻¹ covalent character makes the lattice energy more exothermic, so ΔsolH is much more endothermic (+65 instead of +5 kJ mol⁻¹); ΔSsurroundings is much more negative, so AgCl is far less soluble than a purely ionic compound would be ΔSsystem = 72.7 + 56.5 − 96.2 = +33.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔSsurroundings = −(+65 × 1000) ÷ 298 = −218 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal = −218 + 33.0 = −185 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Kc = [Ag⁺(aq)][Cl⁻(aq)] ln K = −185 ÷ 8.31 = −22.3, so Kc = 2.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ (mol² dm⁻⁶) solubility = √Kc = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ ΔStotal for dissolving AgCl is negative (Kc is very small), so Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ ions cannot stay in solution together and AgCl precipitates (precipitation has a positive ΔStotal); for AgF ΔStotal is positive, so the ions stay in solution and there is no precipitate

items.question: The enthalpy changes of hydration of the halide ions become less exothermic from F⁻ to I⁻. Which is the best explanation for this trend? The ionic radius increases, so the attraction between the ion and the δ+ hydrogen atoms of water molecules decreases. The ionic radius increases, so the attraction between the ion and the δ− oxygen atoms of water molecules decreases. The atomic radius increases, so fewer hydrogen bonds form between the halogen atoms and water molecules. The charge on the ion decreases, so the attraction between the ion and water molecules decreases.
items.ms: A: a halide ion attracts the δ+ hydrogen atoms of water molecules; a larger ion has a lower charge density, so the ion–dipole attraction, and the energy released, are smaller. B: anions attract the δ+ hydrogen, not the δ− oxygen. C refers to atoms and hydrogen bonding, not ions. D: every halide ion has the same 1− charge.
items.why: C12.18 is in 12 of 18 sessions, mostly as cation and lattice-energy MCQs; the hydration of anions and the direction of the water dipole have not been asked, and the examiner reports flag atom/ion confusion.

items.question: In which reaction does the hydrogencarbonate ion, HCO₃⁻, act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid? HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) → H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) HCO₃⁻(aq) + CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq) HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

items.question: Ethanedioic acid, shown below, is a diprotic acid found in rhubarb leaves. It dissociates in two steps. Write equations, with state symbols, for the two successive dissociations of ethanedioic acid in water. items.name: Strong against weak acids: degree of dissociation
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria
C14.6 - the difference between a str
items.question: A student compares hydrochloric acid with butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH. Both solutions have a concentration of 0.100 mol dm⁻³. pKa(butanoic acid) = 4.82 at 298 K Explain, in terms of dissociation, the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid. Include an equation for the dissociation of each of these two acids in water. Calculate the pH of each solution at 298 K. 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid 0.100 mol dm⁻³ butanoic acid Calculate the percentage of butanoic acid molecules that are dissociated in the 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution. The student adds 50.0 cm³ of each acid to separate flasks, each containing an excess of magnesium ribbon, and measures the volume of hydrogen given off. Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g) The graph shows the results for hydrochloric acid. Sketch, on the graph, the curve you would expect for 50.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ butanoic acid. Explain the similarities and differences between the curves for the two acids. Your answer should refer to the dissociation of each acid. pKa(2-chlorobutanoic acid) = 2.86 Explain why 2-chlorobutanoic acid is a stronger acid than butanoic acid. The student then repeats the magnesium experiment with 50.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid that has the same pH as the 0.100 mol dm⁻³ butanoic acid. Calculate the concentration of this hydrochloric acid. Compare the initial rate of reaction and the final volume of hydrogen with those for the butanoic acid. Give reasons for your answers.
items.ms: A strong acid is (almost) completely / fully dissociated in solution A weak acid is only partially / slightly dissociated (most molecules remain undissociated) HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) and CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃CH₂CH₂COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) pH = −log 0.100 = 1.00 Ka = 10−4.82 = 1.51 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ and [H⁺] = √(1.51 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100) = 1.23 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ pH = 2.91 % dissociated = 1.23 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.100 × 100 = 1.23 % Curve starting at the origin with a much less steep initial gradient than the hydrochloric acid curve Curve levelling off at the same final volume (60 cm³), reached later IC1 Both flasks contain the same amount of acid, 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol (same volume and concentration) IC2 HCl is fully dissociated, so [H⁺] at the start is 0.100 mol dm⁻³ IC3 Butanoic acid is only about 1 % dissociated, so its initial [H⁺] is much lower (about 1.2 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³) IC4 Rate depends on [H⁺] / on the frequency of collisions of H⁺ ions with the magnesium surface, so the initial rate (gradient) is much lower for butanoic acid IC5 As H⁺ ions are used up, the equilibrium CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH ⇌ CH₃CH₂CH₂COO⁻ + H⁺ shifts to the right, so more butanoic acid dissociates and replaces them IC6 Eventually all the butanoic acid reacts; with magnesium in excess both acids give the same amount of hydrogen (2.50 × 10⁻³ mol, 60 cm³), but butanoic acid takes longer Chlorine is (highly) electronegative / electron-withdrawing (negative inductive effect) so it weakens the O–H bond / stabilises the carboxylate anion by spreading its negative charge, so the acid dissociates more [HCl] = [H⁺] = 10−2.91 = 1.23 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ Initial rates (about) the same, because the initial [H⁺] is the same Butanoic acid gives far more hydrogen (about 80 times more), because it contains far more acid / its undissociated molecules dissociate as H⁺ is used up
items.why: C14.6 has come up in 12 of 18 sessions (last Jan2026); comparing a strong and a weak acid of equal concentration, and of equal pH, by their reaction with magnesium has not been asked in WCH14, and the 6-mark slot went to acid-base in Jun2024.

path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Which is the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of the hydrogensulfate ion, HSO₄⁻? Ka = [H⁺][SO₄²⁻] / [HSO₄⁻] Ka = [H⁺][HSO₄⁻] / [H₂SO₄] Ka = [H⁺]²[SO₄²⁻] / [H₂SO₄] Ka = [H₃O⁺][SO₄²⁻] / ([HSO₄⁻][H₂O])
items.ms: A: HSO₄⁻(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq), so Ka = [H⁺][SO₄²⁻] / [HSO₄⁻]. B is Ka for H₂SO₄ (its first dissociation), not for HSO₄⁻. C is the overall constant for both dissociations of H₂SO₄. D includes water, which is in large excess and never appears in Ka.
items.why: C14.8 has come up in 12 of 18 sessions, always for a neutral carboxylic acid (Oct2025 Q10(a)(iii)); an ion acting as the weak acid has not been asked, and the ER notes candidates include water.

items.name: The expression for Ka
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria
C14.8 - be able to deduce the expression for the acid diss
items.question: Hydrogen cyanide, HCN, is a very weak acid. pKa(HCN) = 9.21 at 298 K Write the equation, with state symbols, for the dissociation of hydrogen cyanide in water. Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of hydrogen cyanide. Calculate the value of Ka for hydrogen cyanide. Include units in your answer. Calculate the concentration of cyanide ions in 0.500 mol dm⁻³ hydrogen cyanide and the percentage of HCN molecules that are dissociated. Hence comment on the assumption that the equilibrium concentration of HCN is equal to its initial concentration. Propanone reacts with hydrogen cyanide to form the compound shown. The reaction is very slow unless a small amount of potassium cyanide, KCN, is added. Use the Ka expression to explain why adding potassium cyanide to aqueous hydrogen cyanide increases the pH. Explain why adding potassium cyanide increases the rate of the reaction between propanone and hydrogen cyanide. Solutions containing cyanide ions must never be acidified. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of cyanide ions with an excess of hydrochloric acid. Use the pKa value to explain why this reaction goes almost to completion.
items.ms: HCN(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + CN⁻(aq) Ka = [H⁺][CN⁻] / [HCN] Ka = 10−9.21 = 6.17 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³ (value and unit) [H⁺] = [CN⁻] and [HCN] ≈ 0.500 mol dm⁻³, so [CN⁻]² = 6.17 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.500 [CN⁻] = 1.76 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ % dissociated = 1.76 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.500 × 100 = 3.5 × 10⁻³ % The assumption is valid / justified because only a tiny fraction (far less than 1 %) of the HCN is dissociated KCN is (fully) dissociated / ionic, so [CN⁻] increases Ka is constant (at constant temperature), so [H⁺] must decrease (the equilibrium shifts to the left) and the pH rises The first step is attack by the nucleophile CN⁻ on the (δ+) carbonyl carbon atom HCN is only very slightly dissociated so [CN⁻] is very low; KCN provides a much higher [CN⁻] CN⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → HCN(aq) / HCN(g) HCN is a very weak acid (very small Ka / large pKa), so CN⁻ accepts protons very readily and (almost) all of it forms HCN
items.why: C14.8 has come up in 12 of 18 sessions, nearly always as a 1-mark expression for a carboxylic acid (Oct2025 Q10(a)(iii), Jun2025 Q17(a)(i)); using the K_{a} expression to predict the effect of adding the conjugate base, and linking HCN's tiny K_{a} to the KCN catalyst in carbonyl addition, has not been asked.

items.question: Methanoic acid has pKa = 3.75 at 298 K. What is the pH of a 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ solution of methanoic acid? 1.88 2.57 3.27 5.15
items.ms: B: Ka = 10−3.75 = 1.78 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³; [H⁺] = √(Ka × 0.0400) = 2.67 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³; pH = 2.57. A is ½pKa, ignoring the concentration. C halves pKa but not −log c (½ × 3.75 + 1.40). D leaves out the square root.

items.name: pH of a weak acid, with assumptions
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria
C14.9 - calculate the pH of a weak a
items.question: The pH of a weak acid is often calculated using [H⁺] = √(Ka × [HA]initial). Ka(ethanoic acid) = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³; Ka(dichloroethanoic acid) = 4.5 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ For which solution is the pH calculated in this way least reliable? 1.00 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid 1.00 mol dm⁻³ dichloroethanoic acid 0.010 mol dm⁻³ dichloroethanoic acid
items.ms: D: the method assumes [HA]equilibrium = [HA]initial, which fails when a large fraction of the acid dissociates (large Ka, low concentration). Fraction dissociated ≈ √(Ka ÷ c): A 0.4 %, B 13 %, C 21 %, D over 100 % (the calculated [H⁺], 2.1 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³, is more than the acid concentration, which is impossible).
items.why: Assumptions came up in Jan2025 Q12 and Jun2025 Q17(a)(iii), and the 6-mark Jun2024 Q19(a)(iv) asked why the formula fails for dichloroethanoic acid; judging when it fails has not been an MCQ.

items.name: pH of a weak acid, with assumptions
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria

items.question: Compound Q is a carboxylic acid used to make fruit flavourings. In the high-resolution mass spectrum of Q, the molecular ion peak is at m/z = 88.0522. Accurate relative atomic masses: ¹H = 1.0078, ¹²C = 12.0000, ¹⁶O = 15.9949 Use the accurate relative atomic masses to show that the molecular formula of Q is C₄H₈O₂ and not C₅H₁₂O, which has the same integer relative molecular mass. The table shows data from the high-resolution proton NMR spectrum of Q. Deduce the structure of Q. Justify your answer by referring to the chemical shifts, relative peak areas and splitting patterns. Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of Q. A solution is made by dissolving 2.20 g of Q in water and making the volume up to 250.0 cm³. pKa(Q) = 4.86 at 298 K; Mr(Q) = 88.0 Calculate the pH of this solution. State two assumptions made in your calculation in (d). Calculate the mass of Q needed to make 500.0 cm³ of a solution with pH 3.20 at 298 K. Q reacts with ethanol in the presence of a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid. Q + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ ester + H₂O Give the name of the ester formed. 0.150 mol of Q and 0.150 mol of ethanol were mixed with the catalyst and left to reach equilibrium at constant temperature. The equilibrium mixture contained 0.0530 mol of Q. Calculate Kc for this reaction. Give units, if any. For the dissociation of Q in water at 298 K, ΔStotal = R ln Ka. Calculate ΔStotal and explain how your answer is consistent with Q being a weak acid. [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹]
items.ms: Mr(C₄H₈O₂) = (4 × 12.0000) + (8 × 1.0078) + (2 × 15.9949) = 88.0522 Mr(C₅H₁₂O) = 88.0885, which does not match 88.0522 Doublet of area 6 at δ 1.20: two equivalent CH₃ groups, each next to a carbon with one H (n + 1 = 2) Septet of area 1 at δ 2.58: CH next to six H (two CH₃ groups) and next to C=O; singlet at δ 11.9: COOH proton (no neighbouring H) Q is (CH₃)₂CHCOOH / 2-methylpropanoic acid Ka = [H⁺][(CH₃)₂CHCOO⁻] / [(CH₃)₂CHCOOH] [Q] = 2.20 ÷ 88.0 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ Ka = 10−4.86 = 1.38 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³; [H⁺] = √(1.38 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100) = 1.17 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ pH = 2.93 [H⁺] = [(CH₃)₂CHCOO⁻] / all the H⁺ ions come from Q (none from the water) [Q] at equilibrium = initial [Q] / the dissociation of Q is negligible [H⁺] = 10−3.20 = 6.31 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ [Q] = [H⁺]² ÷ Ka = (6.31 × 10⁻⁴)² ÷ 1.38 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.0288 mol dm⁻³ mass = 0.0288 × 0.5000 × 88.0 = 1.27 g ethyl 2-methylpropanoate Equilibrium amounts: Q 0.0530, ethanol 0.0530, ester 0.0970, water 0.0970 mol Kc = [ester][H₂O] ÷ [Q][CH₃CH₂OH] = (0.0970/V)² ÷ (0.0530/V)² Kc = 3.35, no units (the volumes and units cancel) ΔStotal = 8.31 × ln(1.38 × 10⁻⁵) = −93.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal is negative, so the equilibrium lies well to the left: only a small fraction of Q dissociates
items.why: C14.9 is the topic's biggest point (15 of 18 sessions, 3.1 % of marks) and sits inside data-rich questions (Jan2022 Q20, Jan2026 Q20); the reverse mass calculation (Oct2022 Q15(d)) and ΔS_{total} = R ln K_{a} have not been combined with identification in one Section C question.

items.question: The ionic product of water, Kw, changes with temperature. H₂O(l) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) Write the expression for the ionic product of water, Kw, and give its units. At 50 °C, Kw = 5.46 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. Calculate the pH of pure water at 50 °C. A student says that pure water at 50 °C is acidic because its pH is less than 7. Explain why the student is wrong. The graph shows how ln Kw varies with 1/T. The gradient of the line is equal to −ΔH/R, where ΔH is the enthalpy change for the dissociation of water. Explain how the graph shows that the dissociation of water is endothermic. Use the graph to calculate ΔH, in kJ mol⁻¹, for the dissociation of water. [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹] Calculate the pH of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide solution at 50 °C.
items.ms: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] mol² dm⁻⁶ [H⁺] = √Kw (because [H⁺] = [OH⁻]) = 2.34 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ pH = 6.63 In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so it is neutral (at any temperature) As temperature increases (1/T decreases), ln Kw and so Kw increase; K increases with temperature only when the forward reaction is endothermic Gradient from two points far apart on the line, e.g. (−29.27 − (−33.85)) ÷ (0.00290 − 0.00360) = −6.54 × 10³ K ΔH = −gradient × R = 6.54 × 10³ × 8.31 = 5.44 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ ΔH = +54 kJ mol⁻¹ (positive sign and unit) pKw = −log(5.46 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 13.26 / [H⁺] = Kw ÷ 0.0100 = 5.46 × 10⁻¹² mol dm⁻³ pH = 13.26 − 2.00 = 11.26
items.why: C14.10 has come up in 11 of 18 sessions, almost always as a 1-mark MCQ on hot water (Jun2025 Q5, Oct2024 Q8); a structured version with an ln K against 1/T graph (as in Oct2022 Q18(c)) for water has not been asked.

items.question: Ethyl ethanoate is hydrolysed by hydroxide ions. CH₃COOCH₂CH₃(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + CH₃CH₂OH(aq) The reaction was followed at 298 K by measuring the pH of a mixture in which the initial concentrations were [OH⁻] = 0.00500 mol dm⁻³ and [CH₃COOCH₂CH₃] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³. Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K. The ethanoate ions formed have no significant effect on the pH. Show that the initial pH of the mixture is 11.70. The graph shows how the pH of the mixture changed during the first 300 s. Use the graph to determine the hydroxide ion concentration at 120 s. Use the graph to show that the reaction is first order with respect to hydroxide ions. Explain why the graph of pH against time is a straight line. Explain why the ethyl ethanoate is used in a large excess. The experiment is repeated at 40 °C with the same initial concentrations. At 40 °C, Kw = 2.92 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. Calculate the initial pH at 40 °C. In a separate experiment, 3.30 g of ethyl ethanoate (Mr = 88.0) is heated under reflux with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide until hydrolysis is complete. The mixture is cooled and made up to 250.0 cm³ with distilled water. Calculate the pH of this solution at 298 K.
items.ms: pOH = −log 0.00500 = 2.30 / [H⁺] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.00500 = 2.00 × 10⁻¹² mol dm⁻³ pH = 14.00 − 2.30 = 11.70 / −log(2.00 × 10⁻¹²) = 11.70 pH at 120 s = 11.10 (±0.02) [OH⁻] = 10−(14.00 − 11.10) = 1.26 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ [OH⁻] halves each time the pH falls by 0.30 (log 2): 5.00 × 10⁻³ → 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ at pH 11.40 pH 11.40 is reached at 60 s and pH 11.10 at 120 s / each fall of 0.30 takes 60 s The half-life is constant (60 s), so the reaction is first order with respect to OH⁻ pH = 14 − pOH, so every halving of [OH⁻] lowers the pH by the same amount (log 2 = 0.30) The half-life is constant, so the pH falls by equal amounts in equal times So that [ester] stays (effectively) constant and the rate depends only on [OH⁻] / only the order with respect to OH⁻ is measured pKw = 13.53 / [H⁺] = 2.92 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.00500 = 5.84 × 10⁻¹² mol dm⁻³ pH = 11.23 n(ester) = 3.30 ÷ 88.0 = 0.0375 mol and n(NaOH) = 0.0500 mol n(OH⁻) left = 0.0125 mol; [OH⁻] = 0.0125 ÷ 0.2500 = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70

items.question: A student measured the pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid and of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid at 298 K. Each solution was then diluted 10, 100 and 1000 times with distilled water and the pH was measured again. The graph shows the results. Explain why the pH of the hydrochloric acid increases by 1.00 for each tenfold dilution, but the pH of the ethanoic acid increases by only about 0.5.
items.ms: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid / is fully dissociated, so [H⁺] = [HCl] and each tenfold dilution decreases [H⁺] by a factor of 10 (so pH = −log[H⁺] rises by 1) Ethanoic acid is a weak acid: on dilution the equilibrium CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ shifts to the right / a greater proportion of the molecules dissociate, so [H⁺] decreases by a factor of less than 10
items.why: C14.13(ii), comparing a strong and a weak acid after 10, 100 and 1000-fold dilution, is named in the spec but has never been set; pH data analysis was last examined in Oct 2025.

items.name: Titration curves: strong/weak monoprotic and diprotic
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ diprotic acid, H₂X, is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. The values of pKa1 and pKa2 for H₂X are far apart, so the titration curve has two vertical sections. At which volume of sodium hydroxide added is the pH of the mixture equal to pKa2? 12.5 cm³ 25.0 cm³ 37.5 cm³ 50.0 cm³
items.ms: The first equivalence point (H₂X → HX⁻) is at 25.0 cm³ and the second (HX⁻ → X²⁻) at 50.0 cm³. Half-way between them, at 37.5 cm³, [HX⁻] = [X²⁻], so pH = pKa2 (C). A (12.5 cm³) is where pH = pKa1; B is the first equivalence point; D is the second equivalence point.
items.why: Diprotic titration curves were set in Jan 2025 (Ka1 and Ka2 read at 12.5 and 37.5 cm³) and May 2024, and diprotic-acid curves recur as MCQs (May 2023, Oct 2024).

items.question: The graph shows how the pH changes when one solution is added from a burette to 25.0 cm³ of another solution. Both solutions have a concentration of 0.100 mol dm⁻³. Which titration gives this curve? ethanoic acid added to sodium hydroxide sodium hydroxide added to ethanoic acid hydrochloric acid added to sodium hydroxide hydrochloric acid added to aqueous ammonia
items.ms: The curve starts at pH 13, so a strong base is in the flask, and the pH falls as acid is added. After the vertical section at 25.0 cm³ it levels off at about pH 5 (a buffer of excess ethanoic acid and ethanoate ions), so the acid added is weak (A). B would rise from about pH 3. C would fall to below pH 2 after the equivalence point, with a longer vertical section. D would start at about pH 11.
items.why: A titration curve has to be identified in most sessions (Jun 2025, Jun 2022 and Jun 2021 MCQs); the Jan 2024 ER reports candidates confused by titrations run in reverse, with acid added to alkali.

items.question: Sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, acts as a diprotic base. It reacts with hydrochloric acid in two stages. The graph shows how the pH changes when 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is added to 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium carbonate at 298 K. Write ionic equations, including state symbols, for the two stages of the reaction. Use the graph to calculate the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, of the sodium carbonate solution. Use the graph to determine the value of Ka for carbonic acid, H₂CO₃. Ka = [H⁺(aq)][HCO₃⁻(aq)] ÷ [H₂CO₃(aq)] Justify your method and show your working on the graph. The table gives information about three indicators. Select a suitable indicator from the table for each end-point. Justify your choices. Calculate the pH of the mixture when 40.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid has been added. Assume that the carbonic acid formed makes no difference to [H⁺]. On the graph, sketch the curve you would expect if the 25.0 cm³ of sodium carbonate solution were replaced by 25.0 cm³ of 0.0880 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide.
items.ms: Stage 1: CO₃²⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → HCO₃⁻(aq) Stage 2: HCO₃⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) / → H₂CO₃(aq) First equivalence point at 11.0 cm³ (or second at 22.0 cm³): amount of HCl = 0.100 × 11.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.10 × 10⁻³ mol = amount of Na₂CO₃ (or 2.20 × 10⁻³ ÷ 2) [Na₂CO₃] = 1.10 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0440 mol dm⁻³ Half-way between the two equivalence points (16.5 cm³), half of the HCO₃⁻ has been converted into H₂CO₃, so [HCO₃⁻] = [H₂CO₃] so Ka = [H⁺] / pH = pKa; pH read at 16.5 cm³ = 6.35 Ka = 10−6.35 = 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ First end-point: phenolphthalein, as it changes colour on the steep section near 11 cm³ (its range, 8.2–10.0, includes the first equivalence pH of about 8.3) Second end-point: methyl orange, as its range (3.2–4.4) lies within the vertical section at 22 cm³ / includes the equivalence pH of about 4 Excess HCl = 0.100 × (40.0 − 22.0) ÷ 1000 = 1.80 × 10⁻³ mol [H⁺] = 1.80 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0650 = 0.0277 mol dm⁻³ pH = 1.56 Starts at pH 12.9 (allow 12.5–13.1) and falls slowly until just before the equivalence point One vertical section only, at 22.0 cm³ Vertical section covers at least pH 10 to pH 4, and the curve then follows the sodium carbonate curve (pH about 1.8 at 30.0 cm³)
items.why: Titration curves have been examined in all 18 sessions; diprotic acids were set in Jan 2025 and May 2024, but the spec's 'diprotic bases', with two end-points needing two different indicators, has not yet appeared.

items.name: Choosing an indicator
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: When potassium hydroxide solution is added to propanoic acid, the vertical section of the titration curve runs from about pH 7 to pH 11. Which indicator is the most suitable for this titration? phenolphthalein, pH range 8.2–10.0 bromothymol blue, pH range 6.0–7.6 methyl red, pH range 4.2–6.3 methyl orange, pH range 3.2–4.4
items.ms: The whole range of phenolphthalein, 8.2–10.0, lies within the vertical section, so it changes colour with one drop at the end-point (A). The range of bromothymol blue (B) starts below pH 7, so it would begin to change before the end-point; methyl red (C) and methyl orange (D) change colour in the buffer region, well before the equivalence point.
items.why: Choosing an indicator from pH ranges has been asked in 16 of 18 sessions, most often as a one-mark MCQ (Oct 2025, Jun 2025, Oct 2024).

path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Methyl red is an indicator, HIn, with pKin = 5.1. HIn(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + In⁻(aq) HIn is red and In⁻ is yellow. What is the ratio [HIn] : [In⁻] in a solution of pH 4.1, and what colour is the indicator? 1 : 10, yellow 1 : 1, orange 10 : 1, red 100 : 1, red
items.ms: Kin = [H⁺][In⁻] ÷ [HIn], so [HIn] ÷ [In⁻] = [H⁺] ÷ Kin = 10−4.1 ÷ 10−5.1 = 10. The red HIn form predominates (C). A inverts the ratio; B is the ratio at pH = pKin (the end-point colour); D treats a difference of one pH unit as a factor of 100.
items.why: Oct 2024 Q7 asked why phenolphthalein, a weak acid, changes colour; using pKin to find the ratio of the two coloured forms is the quantitative version, not yet set.

path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

C14.16 - select a suitable indicator
items.question: The graph shows the titration curves obtained when 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is added to 25.0 cm³ of three different acids, P, Q and R, each of concentration 0.100 mol dm⁻³. The acids are hydrochloric acid, butanoic acid (pKa = 4.82) and a very weak acid, HZ (pKa = 9.20). Some indicators are shown in the table. Identify which acid is P, which is Q and which is R. Justify your answer using the starting pH of the curves. Explain why phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for titration Q but methyl orange is not. State the colour of the solution at the end-point if bromothymol blue is used in titration P. Explain why none of the indicators in the table would give an accurate end-point in titration R. Phenolphthalein is a weak acid, HIn. HIn(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + In⁻(aq) HIn is colourless and In⁻ is pink. Explain why phenolphthalein is colourless at the start of titration Q but pink when excess sodium hydroxide has been added.
items.ms: P = hydrochloric acid, Q = butanoic acid and R = HZ (all three needed) The weaker the acid, the smaller its degree of dissociation, so the lower [H⁺] and the higher the starting pH (P about 1, Q about 2.9, R about 5.1) The pH range of phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) lies (completely) within the vertical section of curve Q (about pH 7 to 11) The pH range of methyl orange (3.2–4.4) is below the vertical section / in the region near the start, so it would change colour gradually, long before the equivalence point (25.0 cm³) Green (a mixture of the yellow and blue forms) There is no (sharp) vertical section on curve R / the pH rises only gradually through the equivalence point (25.0 cm³) so any indicator would change colour gradually over a large volume of sodium hydroxide / the end-point could not be seen at one drop At the start [H⁺] is high, so the equilibrium lies to the left and the colourless HIn form predominates Added OH⁻ ions remove H⁺ (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O), so the equilibrium shifts to the right and the pink In⁻ form predominates
items.why: Indicator choice has come up in 16 of 18 sessions (mostly one-mark MCQs); the ERs single out 'range within the vertical section' and the end-point colour, and a very weak acid with no usable end-point has not yet been set.

items.name: What a buffer is

items.question: Buffer solutions are used in many areas of chemistry and biology. State what is meant by the term buffer solution. A mixture of hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride contains the acid HCl and its conjugate base Cl⁻. Explain why this mixture is not a buffer solution.
items.ms: A solution that resists changes in pH / whose pH stays almost constant when small amounts of acid or of alkali are added HCl is a strong acid / fully dissociated, so there is no reservoir of undissociated acid to remove added OH⁻ / Cl⁻ is too weak a base to remove added H⁺

items.question: A buffer solution contains sodium dihydrogenphosphate, NaH₂PO₄, and disodium hydrogenphosphate, Na₂HPO₄. Which equation shows how this buffer removes a small amount of added acid? H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₃PO₄(aq) HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₂PO₄⁻(aq) H₂PO₄⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → HPO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) HPO₄²⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → PO₄³⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
items.ms: In the H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻ pair the base, HPO₄²⁻, accepts the added H⁺ (B). A adds H⁺ to the acid of the pair (a common error); C shows how the buffer removes added alkali; D involves PO₄³⁻, which is not part of this buffer.
items.why: Buffer action has been tested in 15 of 18 sessions, phosphate buffers in Oct 2020 and Jan 2026; the ERs report H⁺ added to the wrong member of the pair (Jan 2021).

path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Four buffer solutions are made from ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate. 1.0 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is added to 100 cm³ of each buffer. Which buffer shows the smallest change in pH? [CH₃COOH] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³, [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ [CH₃COOH] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³, [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³ [CH₃COOH] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³, [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³ [CH₃COOH] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³, [CH₃COO⁻] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³
items.ms: The 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol of H⁺ converts CH₃COO⁻ into CH₃COOH. The pH depends on the ratio [CH₃COOH] : [CH₃COO⁻], which changes least when both amounts are large: in D the ratio goes from 1.00 to 1.04, so ΔpH = −0.02 (D). The pH of A changes by −0.09, C by −0.11 and B, with the smallest reservoirs, by −0.18.
items.why: Mark schemes for buffer action (Jan 2026, Jun 2023) now reward the 'ratio changes only slightly' argument; how the size of the reservoirs affects the pH change has not been tested.

items.name: Buffer action
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria
C14.18 - the action of a buffer solut
items.question: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, is used in the dyeing of wool. The pH of a dye bath is controlled with a buffer solution made from methanoic acid and sodium methanoate, HCOONa. [Ka for methanoic acid = 1.78 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K] Explain how a methanoic acid–sodium methanoate buffer keeps its pH almost constant when small amounts of acid or of alkali are added, and why its pH hardly changes when it is diluted with water. Include relevant equations in your answer. Calculate the pH of a buffer solution containing 0.150 mol dm⁻³ methanoic acid and 0.250 mol dm⁻³ sodium methanoate. 1.00 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is added to 100 cm³ of the buffer solution in (b). Calculate the new pH of the buffer solution.
items.ms: IC1 Methanoic acid is a weak acid, only slightly dissociated: HCOOH ⇌ HCOO⁻ + H⁺ IC2 Sodium methanoate is fully ionised, so there are large reservoirs of both HCOOH and HCOO⁻ IC3 Added H⁺ ions are removed by methanoate ions: HCOO⁻ + H⁺ → HCOOH IC4 Added OH⁻ ions are removed by methanoic acid: HCOOH + OH⁻ → HCOO⁻ + H₂O (or H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O and more HCOOH dissociates) IC5 [H⁺] = Ka × [HCOOH] ÷ [HCOO⁻]; as both concentrations are large, the ratio [HCOOH] : [HCOO⁻] changes only slightly, so the pH changes only slightly IC6 On dilution, [HCOOH] and [HCOO⁻] decrease by the same factor, so the ratio, and hence [H⁺] and the pH, stay (almost) the same [H⁺] = Ka × [HCOOH] ÷ [HCOO⁻] [H⁺] = 1.78 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.150 ÷ 0.250 = 1.068 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ pH = 3.97 Initial amounts in 100 cm³: HCOOH = 0.0150 mol, HCOO⁻ = 0.0250 mol; NaOH added = 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol After reaction: HCOOH = 0.0140 mol and HCOO⁻ = 0.0260 mol [H⁺] = 1.78 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.0140 ÷ 0.0260 = 9.58 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 4.02
items.why: Buffer action has been examined in 15 of 18 sessions (most recently Jan 2026); mark schemes reward the reservoir, both equations and the ratio argument, and the effect of dilution on a buffer has not been asked.

items.name: Calculating the pH of a buffer
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: A buffer solution contains 0.20 mol dm⁻³ butanoic acid and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium butanoate. pKa of butanoic acid = 4.82 What is the pH of this buffer solution? 4.13 4.52 4.82 5.12
items.ms: [H⁺] = Ka × [acid] ÷ [salt] = 10−4.82 × 0.20 ÷ 0.10 = 3.03 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³, pH = 4.52 (B). A uses ln instead of log; C is pKa alone (as if the concentrations were equal); D inverts the ratio.
items.why: A buffer-pH MCQ appeared in Oct 2025, Jan 2025, May 2024, Oct 2022 and Oct 2020; the Jan 2025 distractors were the inverted ratio, the bare pKa and a natural log.

items.question: 30.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is added to 40.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid. pKa of ethanoic acid = 4.76 What is the pH of the mixture? 4.28 4.64 4.76 5.24
items.ms: Amounts: CH₃COOH 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol, OH⁻ 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol, leaving 1.00 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COOH and 3.00 × 10⁻³ mol CH₃COO⁻. pH = 4.76 + log(3.00 ÷ 1.00) = 5.24 (D). A inverts the ratio; B uses the starting amount of acid (4.00 × 10⁻³ mol) with the ethanoate; C is pKa, which is true only at half-neutralisation.
items.why: Making a buffer by part-neutralising a weak acid was set in Oct 2025 Q5(d) and Jan 2020 Q20(b); the Jan 2020 ER says candidates used the starting amount of acid.

items.question: Calcium propanoate, (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca, is added to bread to stop mould growing. In the dough it forms a mixture of propanoic acid and propanoate ions. [Ka for propanoic acid = 1.35 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K] Propanoic acid can be made by oxidising propan-1-ol. Give the reagents and conditions for this reaction, and the colour change seen. Calcium propanoate can be made by reacting propanoic acid with calcium carbonate. Write the equation for this reaction. Include state symbols. A buffer solution is made by dissolving 3.00 g of calcium propanoate in 500 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid. Assume that the volume of the solution does not change. [Mr of (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca = 186.1] Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of propanoic acid. Calculate the pH of the buffer solution. Explain why less calcium propanoate is needed to stop mould growing in sourdough bread than in ordinary bread. Calculate ΔStotal, in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, for the dissociation of propanoic acid at 298 K, using the expression ΔStotal = R ln K. At 323 K, Ka for propanoic acid is 1.32 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Deduce whether the dissociation of propanoic acid is exothermic or endothermic. Justify your answer.
items.ms: Potassium dichromate(VI) and sulfuric acid / acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ Heat under reflux (with excess oxidising agent) Orange to green 2CH₃CH₂COOH + CaCO₃ → (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂ (formulae and balancing) State symbols: CH₃CH₂COOH(aq), CaCO₃(s), (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca(aq), H₂O(l), CO₂(g) Ka = [CH₃CH₂COO⁻(aq)][H⁺(aq)] ÷ [CH₃CH₂COOH(aq)] amount of (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca = 3.00 ÷ 186.1 = 0.01612 mol [CH₃CH₂COO⁻] = 2 × 0.01612 ÷ 0.500 = 0.0645 mol dm⁻³ [H⁺] = Ka × [CH₃CH₂COOH] ÷ [CH₃CH₂COO⁻] = 1.35 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100 ÷ 0.0645 = 2.09 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ pH = 4.68 [H⁺] = 10−5.50 = 3.16 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ [CH₃CH₂COOH] ÷ [CH₃CH₂COO⁻] = [H⁺] ÷ Ka = 3.16 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 1.35 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.234 percentage = 0.234 ÷ 1.234 × 100 = 19.0% At lower pH, [H⁺] is higher, so the equilibrium CH₃CH₂COO⁻ + H⁺ ⇌ CH₃CH₂COOH lies further to the right / the ratio [CH₃CH₂COOH] : [CH₃CH₂COO⁻] = [H⁺] : Ka is larger so a greater proportion (about 70%) is present as propanoic acid molecules, which stop mould growing ln K = ln (1.35 × 10⁻⁵) = −11.21 ΔStotal = 8.31 × (−11.213) = −93.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Ka decreases as the temperature increases / the position of equilibrium moves to the left (towards undissociated acid) on heating so the forward reaction (dissociation) is exothermic
items.why: Buffer pH calculations have appeared in 15 of 18 sessions (most recently Jan 2026, from masses); a salt that gives two anions per formula unit and the fraction of acid left undissociated have not been set, and Section C questions regularly bring in organic preparations and ΔS_total = R ln K.

items.question: The graph shows how the pH changes when 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is added from a burette to 25.0 cm³ of aqueous ammonia, NH₃(aq), at 298 K. Use the graph to find the volume of hydrochloric acid needed to neutralise the ammonia. Hence calculate the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, of the aqueous ammonia. Explain why the pH at the equivalence point is less than 7. Between about 4 cm³ and 20 cm³ of acid added, the pH falls only slowly. Explain, with the help of an equation, why the mixture behaves as a buffer in this region. Use the graph to determine the value of Ka for the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. Show your working on the graph.
items.ms: Volume at the equivalence point (middle of the vertical section) = 24.0 cm³ [NH₃] = 0.100 × 24.0 ÷ 25.0 = 0.0960 mol dm⁻³ The solution contains NH₄⁺ ions, which are a weak acid / donate protons: NH₄⁺(aq) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H⁺(aq) or NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) The mixture contains large amounts / a reservoir of both NH₃ and NH₄⁺ (a weak base and its conjugate acid) Added H⁺ ions are removed by ammonia: NH₃(aq) + H⁺(aq) → NH₄⁺(aq) so the ratio [NH₄⁺] : [NH₃] changes only slightly, and the pH changes only slightly At half the equivalence volume (12.0 cm³), [NH₄⁺] = [NH₃], so pH = pKa(NH₄⁺) = 9.25 Ka = 10−9.25 = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³
items.why: Half-neutralisation → pKa was set in Oct 2023, Jan 2024, Jan 2025 and Jun 2022, always for a weak acid and a strong base; the spec also names the strong acid–weak base curve (pKa of NH₄⁺), not yet asked.

items.name: Buffers in cells, blood and food
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria

items.question: The pH of blood plasma is kept close to 7.40 mainly by the carbonic acid–hydrogencarbonate buffer. H₂CO₃(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq) At pH 7.40 the ratio [HCO₃⁻] : [H₂CO₃] in blood is about 20 : 1. Metabolism releases much more acid into the blood (for example carbon dioxide and lactic acid) than alkali. Explain why, on its own, this buffer can remove much more added acid than added alkali.
items.ms: There is a large reservoir of HCO₃⁻ (about twenty times [H₂CO₃]) to remove added H⁺: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃ There is only a small amount of H₂CO₃ to remove added OH⁻ (H₂CO₃ + OH⁻ → HCO₃⁻ + H₂O), so it would be used up / the ratio would change greatly after a much smaller amount of alkali
items.why: Blood buffering was set in Jan 2026, Jan 2025, May 2024 and Jun 2021; the 20 : 1 ratio appears in mark schemes but its effect on how much acid or alkali the buffer can take up has not been asked.

C14.23 - CORE PRACTICAL 11 Finding the Ka value for a
items.question: Lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid), CH₃CH(OH)COOH, is a weak monoprotic acid found in sour milk. Its skeletal formula is shown. On the skeletal formula, mark the chiral centre with an asterisk (*). Lactic acid from sour milk is mainly one enantiomer, but lactic acid made in the laboratory is a racemic mixture. Explain whether the two samples would have different values of Ka. Write an equation for the reaction of lactic acid with sodium hydroxide. State symbols are not required. A student used this method to find Ka for a solution of lactic acid at 298 K. Step 1 Calibrate a pH meter. Step 2 Pipette 25.0 cm³ of the lactic acid solution into a conical flask, add a few drops of phenolphthalein and titrate with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. Repeat until concordant titres are obtained. Step 3 Measure the pH of the lactic acid solution. pH = 2.47 Step 4 Pipette 25.0 cm³ of the lactic acid solution into a beaker and add the mean titre of sodium hydroxide from a burette. Then add a further 25.0 cm³ of the lactic acid solution, stir and measure the pH. pH = 3.88 The results of Step 2 are shown in the table. Calculate the mean titre, using only concordant results. Calculate the concentration, in mol dm⁻³, of the lactic acid solution. Explain why phenolphthalein (pH range 8.2–10.0) is used in Step 2 rather than methyl orange (pH range 3.2–4.4). Describe how the pH meter is calibrated in Step 1. Step 4 gives one value of Ka. Explain why the pH measured in Step 4 is equal to pKa of lactic acid. Calculate the value of Ka for lactic acid from Step 4. Include units. Step 3 gives a second value of Ka. Use the pH in Step 3 and your answer to (d)(ii) to calculate a second value of Ka. Calculate the percentage of lactic acid molecules that are dissociated in the solution in Step 3. The pH meter readings are uncertain by ±0.02. Evaluate which step, Step 3 or Step 4, gives the more reliable value of Ka. Justify your answer.
items.ms: Asterisk on the carbon atom bonded to the OH group (carbon 2) No / the same Ka: enantiomers have identical chemical properties (except in reactions with other chiral molecules), so the –COOH group dissociates to the same extent CH₃CH(OH)COOH + NaOH → CH₃CH(OH)COONa + H₂O Titres: rough 24.10; 1, 2 and 3: 23.55, 23.45, 23.80 cm³; the concordant titres are 1 and 2 (they differ by only 0.10 cm³; titration 3 differs from both by 0.25 cm³ or more) Mean titre = (23.55 + 23.45) ÷ 2 = 23.50 cm³ amount of NaOH = 0.100 × 23.50 ÷ 1000 = 2.35 × 10⁻³ mol = amount of lactic acid [lactic acid] = 2.35 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0940 mol dm⁻³ This is a weak acid–strong base titration, so the vertical section (and the equivalence point) is in the alkaline region, about pH 7 to 11 The range of phenolphthalein lies within the vertical section but that of methyl orange does not (it would change colour gradually in the buffer region, before the end-point) Place the electrode in buffer solution(s) of known pH (for example pH 4.00 and pH 7.00) and adjust the meter to read the pH of each buffer Rinse the electrode with distilled (deionised) water between solutions Use buffers with pH values close to / either side of the pH values to be measured The mean titre exactly neutralises one 25.0 cm³ portion, so after the second portion is added half of the total lactic acid has been neutralised / the mixture contains equal amounts of lactic acid and lactate ions Ka = [H⁺][lactate] ÷ [lactic acid], and as [lactate] = [lactic acid], Ka = [H⁺], so pH = pKa Ka = 10−3.88 = 1.32 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ [H⁺] = 10−2.47 = 3.39 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ Ka = [H⁺]² ÷ [lactic acid] = (3.39 × 10⁻³)² ÷ 0.0940 = 1.22 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ 3.39 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0940 × 100 = 3.6% Step 3 uses [H⁺]², so the ±0.02 uncertainty in pH has twice the effect on Ka (about ±10% compared with about ±5% for Step 4) Step 3 assumes that [lactic acid] at equilibrium equals the initial concentration, but 3.6% of the acid is dissociated Step 3 also depends on the concentration found by titration, whereas Step 4 does not need the concentration of the acid so Step 4 gives the more reliable value (1.32 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³)
items.why: Core Practical 11 has never been examined as a practical (0 of 18 sessions), though its half-neutralisation idea underlies Oct 2023, Jan 2024 and Jan 2025 parts; the Jan 2024 ER says many candidates did not see that pH = pKa at half-neutralisation despite having done the practical.

items.question: Nitramide, NH₂NO₂, decomposes in aqueous solution. NH₂NO₂(aq) → N₂O(g) + H₂O(l) In alkaline solution, the rate equation for the reaction is rate = k[NH₂NO₂][OH⁻] What are the overall order of the reaction and the units of the rate constant, k? overall order 1; units of k: s⁻¹ overall order 1; units of k: dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ overall order 2; units of k: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ overall order 2; units of k: dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
items.ms: The order is the sum of the powers in the rate equation (1 + 1 = 2), including OH⁻, which catalyses the reaction although it is not in the overall equation; k = rate ÷ ([NH₂NO₂][OH⁻]) = mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ ÷ (mol dm⁻³)² = dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. A counts only the species in the overall equation; B gives second-order units for a first-order reaction; C gives the units of rate (correct only for zero order).
items.why: C11.1 MCQs on order and units of k recur (Jan2022 Q4, Jun2024 Q1(b), Oct2025 Q2(b)); a catalyst that appears in the rate equation but not in the overall equation (examined in Oct2024 Q18) has not yet been an MCQ.

items.question: Hydrogen peroxide oxidises iodide ions in acidic solution. H₂O₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → I₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l) Under the conditions used, the rate equation is rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻] In a second experiment at the same temperature, the concentration of hydrogen peroxide is halved, the concentration of iodide ions is tripled and the concentration of hydrogen ions is doubled. By what factor does the initial rate change? × 1.5 × 3.0 × 4.5 × 18
items.ms: Rate ∝ [H₂O₂][I⁻] and is independent of [H⁺] (zero order), so the factor is ½ × 3 = 1.5. B treats H⁺ as first order (½ × 3 × 2); C uses the coefficient of I⁻ as its order (½ × 3²); D uses every coefficient in the overall equation as an order (½ × 3² × 2²).
items.why: Rate-factor MCQs appeared in Jun2025 Q10, Jun2024 Q1(c), Oct2023 Q2 and Oct2022 Q2(a); a reactant that is zero order is the likeliest new twist.

items.question: Sulfuryl chloride decomposes in a first-order reaction. SO₂Cl₂(g) → SO₂(g) + Cl₂(g) At 593 K, the partial pressure of SO₂Cl₂ falls from 48.0 kPa to 6.0 kPa in 26.4 hours. What is the half-life of the reaction at 593 K? 3.3 hours 6.6 hours 8.8 hours 13.2 hours
items.ms: 48.0 → 24.0 → 12.0 → 6.0 kPa is three half-lives, so t½ = 26.4 ÷ 3 = 8.8 hours (constant for a first-order reaction). A divides by 8 (one-eighth remains); B divides by 4; D divides by 2, as if one half-life had passed.
items.why: C11.2 MCQs appear in most sessions (Jan2024 Q2 asked for the concentration after three half-lives); working back from the time taken to reach one-eighth is the reverse form, not yet asked.

items.question: Methoxymethane decomposes when it is heated to 777 K in a sealed container. CH₃OCH₃(g) → CH₄(g) + H₂(g) + CO(g) The graph shows how the concentration of methoxymethane changes with time. Use the graph to show that the reaction is first order with respect to methoxymethane. Show your working on the graph. The rate constant of a first-order reaction is given by k = 0.693 ÷ t½. Calculate the value of k for this reaction, in s⁻¹.
items.ms: Two half-lives shown on the graph, e.g. 8.0 → 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ in 25 min and 4.0 → 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ in a further 25 min (each 24–26 min) The half-life is constant, so the reaction is first order t½ converted to seconds: 25 × 60 = 1500 s k = 0.693 ÷ 1500 = 4.62 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹

items.question: A student wants to follow the rates of two reactions by measuring the loss in mass of an open flask and its contents on a balance that reads to 0.01 g. Reaction 1 CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) Reaction 2 Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) In each experiment, 0.0100 mol of the solid reacts completely with excess acid. Justify, using a calculation, why measuring the loss in mass is suitable for reaction 1 but not for reaction 2. [Mr values: CO₂ = 44.0, H₂ = 2.0]

items.question: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes in the presence of aqueous potassium iodide. 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) At time zero, a student mixed solutions of hydrogen peroxide and potassium iodide to give 25.0 cm³ of a mixture in which the initial concentration of hydrogen peroxide was 0.150 mol dm⁻³. The flask was connected to a gas syringe and the volume of oxygen was recorded every 30 s. The graph shows the results. Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0 and use it to determine the initial rate of formation of oxygen, in cm³ s⁻¹. Calculate the initial rate of decrease of the concentration of hydrogen peroxide, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. [Molar volume of a gas under the conditions of the experiment = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹] The student wants to use an initial-rate method to find the order of reaction with respect to iodide ions. Describe how the experiment should be repeated and how the results should be used to find the order. Details of the apparatus are not required.
items.ms: Tangent drawn to the curve at t = 0 Gradient of the tangent calculated: initial rate = 0.26 cm³ s⁻¹ (range 0.23–0.29) mol O₂ formed per second = 0.26 ÷ 24 000 = 1.08 × 10⁻⁵ (mol s⁻¹) mol H₂O₂ used per second = 2 × 1.08 × 10⁻⁵ = 2.17 × 10⁻⁵ (mol s⁻¹) rate = 2.17 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.0250 = 8.67 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ Repeat with different initial concentrations of iodide ions, e.g. different volumes of potassium iodide solution Keep the initial concentration of hydrogen peroxide, the total volume (by adding water) and the temperature the same Find the initial rate of each experiment from the gradient of a tangent at t = 0 Plot initial rate against [I⁻]: a straight line through the origin / rate doubling when [I⁻] doubles shows first order (a horizontal line shows zero order)
items.why: C11.4's own questions have all been clock reactions (Jan2023 Q17, Jan2024 Q16, Jan2025 Q18(b)); the continuous-monitoring half of the point, a tangent at t = 0 on a volume–time graph (Jun2024 Q16(a)(i), Jan2025 Q18(c)), with conversion to mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, is the likeliest fresh angle.

items.question: The graphs show how the rate, or the concentration of a reactant Q, changes in four different reactions. Which graph shows a reaction that is second order with respect to Q? graph A graph B graph C graph D
items.ms: For a second-order reaction rate = k[Q]², so rate against [Q] is a curve through the origin that gets steeper. A is first order (rate ∝ [Q]); C is zero order (rate does not depend on [Q]); D, a straight-line fall in [Q] with time, is also zero order.
items.why: Graph-shape MCQs recur (Jan2026 Q1(b), Oct2025 Q2(c), Jun2022 Q10(a)) and have always keyed zero or first order; the second-order rate–concentration curve has not yet been the answer.

items.question: X and Y react: X + 2Y → XY₂ The table shows initial-rate data at constant temperature. What are the orders of reaction with respect to X and to Y? second order in X, first order in Y second order in X, second order in Y first order in X, second order in Y first order in X, first order in Y
items.ms: Experiments 1 and 2: [X] × 3 at constant [Y] and the rate × 9, so second order in X. Experiments 1 and 3: [X] × 2 alone would give × 4, but the rate is × 8, so doubling [Y] doubles the rate: first order in Y. B would give × 16 for experiment 3; C uses the coefficients in the equation; D would give × 3 for experiment 2.

items.question: Ethyl ethanoate is hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide at 298 K. CH₃COOC₂H₅(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + C₂H₅OH(aq) Name the two organic products of this reaction. In experiment 1, the initial concentrations were [CH₃COOC₂H₅] = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and [OH⁻] = 0.100 mol dm⁻³. Samples were removed at intervals and the concentration of ethyl ethanoate in each sample was found. The graph shows the results. Each sample was added to an excess of cold dilute hydrochloric acid as soon as it was removed. Explain why. Draw tangents to the curve at [CH₃COOC₂H₅] = 4.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and at 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Use their gradients to deduce the order of reaction with respect to ethyl ethanoate. In experiments 2 to 6, the initial concentration of ethyl ethanoate was 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ each time and the initial concentration of hydroxide ions was changed. The initial rates are shown in the table. Plot a graph of initial rate against [OH⁻] on the grid. Deduce the order of reaction with respect to hydroxide ions. Justify your answer. Write the rate equation for the reaction. Use the gradient of your graph to calculate the value of the rate constant, k. Include units in your answer. In experiment 1 the half-life of ethyl ethanoate was 60 s. Predict the half-life of ethyl ethanoate in an experiment that is the same as experiment 1 except that [OH⁻] = 0.200 mol dm⁻³. Explain your answer. Deduce the species involved in the rate-determining step of the mechanism. Justify your answer. Calculate the pH of a solution in which [OH⁻] = 0.250 mol dm⁻³, as at the start of experiment 6. [Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶] Ethyl ethanoate can also be hydrolysed by heating it under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid. Explain why hydrolysis with sodium hydroxide goes to completion but hydrolysis with the acid does not.
items.ms: ethanoate ion / sodium ethanoate and ethanol (both needed) The acid neutralises the hydroxide ions, so the reaction stops / is quenched at the time the sample is taken (and cooling slows it) Both tangents drawn and gradients calculated, about 4.6 × 10⁻⁵ and 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (in the ratio about 2 : 1) Halving the concentration halves the rate, so the reaction is first order with respect to ethyl ethanoate Axes the correct way round, labelled with units, and a scale on which the points cover at least half the grid in each direction All five points plotted correctly (± half a small square) Straight line of best fit passing through (or very close to) the origin First order, because the graph is a straight line through the origin / the rate is directly proportional to [OH⁻] rate = k[CH₃COOC₂H₅][OH⁻] Gradient of the line calculated, e.g. 5.8 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (range 5.5–6.1 × 10⁻⁴) k = gradient ÷ [CH₃COOC₂H₅] = gradient ÷ 5.00 × 10⁻³ k = 0.116 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (range 0.110–0.122; value and units) 30 s The reaction is first order in OH⁻ and [OH⁻] stays (almost) constant because it is in large excess, so the rate is doubled at every ester concentration and the concentration halves in half the time One molecule of ethyl ethanoate and one hydroxide ion Because the reaction is first order with respect to each of them / each appears in the rate equation to the power one [H⁺] = Kw ÷ [OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.250 = 4.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ (mol dm⁻³) pH = 13.40 Acid hydrolysis is reversible / reaches equilibrium because the ethanoic acid and ethanol formed react to re-form the ester With sodium hydroxide the acid is converted into the ethanoate ion, which does not react with ethanol, so the reverse reaction cannot occur
items.why: C11.5 is hot (17 of 18 sessions, 3.6% of marks); initial-rate tables recur, while plotting a rate–concentration graph and using its gradient (Jan2025 Q18(b)) and rates from tangents on a concentration–time curve are the rarer forms likely to return.

items.name: Acid-catalysed iodination of propanone: obtaining data and deducing the mechanism
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.6 - how to i obtain data to calc
items.question: Propanone reacts with iodine in the presence of an acid catalyst. CH₃COCH₃(aq) + I₂(aq) → CH₃COCH₂I(aq) + H⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) A student followed the reaction using a colorimeter. Explain why colorimetry can be used to follow this reaction. In experiment 1, the initial concentrations were [CH₃COCH₃] = 0.800 mol dm⁻³, [H⁺] = 0.500 mol dm⁻³ and [I₂] = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. The absorbance is directly proportional to the concentration of iodine, and was 0.80 at t = 0. The graph shows the results. Explain why propanone and acid were used in large excess. Deduce the order of reaction with respect to iodine. Justify your answer. Calculate the rate of reaction in experiment 1, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The student then measured the initial rates of three more experiments, each with iodine in a small concentration. Deduce the rate equation for the reaction. Justify your answer using the data. Explain what the rate equation suggests about the rate-determining step of the mechanism.
items.ms: Iodine is the only coloured species (yellow-brown); the other reactants and products are colourless, so the absorbance falls as iodine is used up So that their concentrations stay (almost) constant, and only the change in iodine concentration can affect the rate Zero order, because the graph is a straight line / the gradient (rate) stays constant as the iodine concentration falls Gradient = (0.80 − 0.20) ÷ 150 = 4.0 × 10⁻³ (absorbance units) s⁻¹ rate = 4.0 × 10⁻³ × (2.00 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.80) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ Experiments 2 and 3: [CH₃COCH₃] doubles at constant [H⁺] and the rate doubles, so first order in propanone Experiments 3 and 4: [H⁺] halves at constant [CH₃COCH₃] and the rate halves, so first order in H⁺; rate = k[CH₃COCH₃][H⁺] The rate-determining step involves propanone and H⁺ (one of each) but not iodine, so iodine reacts in a (fast) step after the rate-determining step
items.why: C11.6 was last examined through the titrimetric method (Oct2025 Q11); following the same reaction by colorimetry is a spec-suggested practical that has not yet been examined.
