items.question: Nitrogen dioxide reacts with fluorine. 2NO₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2NO₂F(g) The mechanism is Step 1 NO₂ + F₂ → NO₂F + F slow Step 2 NO₂ + F → NO₂F fast What is the rate equation for the reaction? rate = k[NO₂]²[F₂] rate = k[NO₂][F₂] rate = k[NO₂][F] rate = k[F₂]
items.ms: Only the species in the slow (rate-determining) step appear in the rate equation: one NO₂ and one F₂. A is written from the overall equation; C uses step 2 and includes the intermediate F; D leaves out NO₂.
items.why: Writing a rate equation from a mechanism with a slow first step recurs (Jan2023 Q3, May2023 Q7, Oct2024 Q18(b)).

items.name: Rate-determining step from a rate equation, and vice versa
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Hydrogen reacts with iodine monochloride. H₂(g) + 2ICl(g) → I₂(g) + 2HCl(g) The rate equation is rate = k[H₂][ICl] A two-step mechanism is proposed. Step 1 H₂ + ICl → HI + HCl Step 2 HI + ICl → I₂ + HCl Which statement is correct? Step 2 is the rate-determining step. HI is a catalyst in this reaction. Step 1 is the rate-determining step. The reaction is third order overall.
items.ms: Step 1 contains one H₂ and one ICl, matching the rate equation, so it is rate-determining. A: step 2 would give rate = k[HI][ICl]. B: HI is an intermediate (formed and then used up), not a catalyst. D: the reaction is second order overall (1 + 1).
items.why: Identifying the rate-determining step is a regular MCQ (Oct2022 Q2(c), Jun2024 Q1(d)); telling an intermediate from a catalyst (Jan2026 Q4(a)) is paired with it here.

items.name: Rate-determining step from a rate equation, and vice versa
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Nitrogen monoxide reacts with bromine. 2NO(g) + Br₂(g) → 2NOBr(g) The rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[Br₂] A two-step mechanism is proposed. Step 1 NO(g) + Br₂(g) → NOBr₂(g) Step 2 NOBr₂(g) + NO(g) → 2NOBr(g) Deduce which step is the rate-determining step. Justify your answer.
items.ms: Step 2 Step 2 involves NOBr₂, which was formed from one NO and one Br₂, and a second NO, so two NO and one Br₂ take part up to and including this step, as in the rate equation / if step 1 were rate-determining the rate equation would be rate = k[NO][Br₂]

items.name: Deducing a mechanism from the rate and stoichiometric equations
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics

items.question: Nitrogen dioxide reacts with ozone. 2NO₂(g) + O₃(g) → N₂O₅(g) + O₂(g) The rate equation is rate = k[NO₂][O₃] Which mechanism is consistent with both the overall equation and the rate equation? 2NO₂ + O₃ → N₂O₅ + O₂ (one step) Step 1 NO₂ + O₃ → NO₃ + O₂ fast; Step 2 NO₃ + NO₂ → N₂O₅ slow Step 1 NO₂ + O₃ → NO₃ + O₂ slow; Step 2 2NO₃ → 2NO₂ + O₂ fast Step 1 NO₂ + O₃ → NO₃ + O₂ slow; Step 2 NO₃ + NO₂ → N₂O₅ fast
items.ms: In D the slow step contains one NO₂ and one O₃, and the two steps add up to the overall equation. A would give rate = k[NO₂]²[O₃] (and needs a three-particle collision); in B the species up to the slow step are 2NO₂ + O₃; in C the slow step fits, but the steps do not add up to the overall equation.
items.why: Choosing a mechanism consistent with both equations was asked in Jan2021 Q7, and the Oct2023 ER says candidates check only one of the two; it is due to return.

items.name: Deducing a mechanism from the rate and stoichiometric equations
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Below 500 K, nitrogen dioxide reacts with carbon monoxide. NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g) The rate equation is rate = k[NO₂]² Suggest a two-step mechanism for this reaction that is consistent with the rate equation and the overall equation. State which step is slow.
items.ms: Slow first step involving two NO₂ and no CO, e.g. 2NO₂ → NO₃ + NO (slow) Fast second step involving CO, so that the two steps add up to the overall equation, e.g. NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂ (fast)
items.why: C11.8 is warm (12 of 18 sessions) but is usually a one-line reason or an MCQ (Jan2022 Q18(b), Jan2026 Q4(b)); writing a mechanism in which a reactant (CO) is absent from the rate equation has not been asked.

items.name: Rate equations as evidence for SN1 and SN2 (primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes)
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.9 - that knowledge of the rate e
items.question: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CClCH₂CH₃, is hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide. In a second experiment at the same temperature, the concentration of 2-chloro-2-methylbutane is halved and the concentration of hydroxide ions is doubled. By what factor does the initial rate change? × 0.25 × 0.5 × 1 × 2
items.ms: A tertiary halogenoalkane is hydrolysed by SN1: rate = k[(CH₃)₂CClCH₂CH₃], so halving its concentration halves the rate and [OH⁻] has no effect. A squares the halving; C assumes SN2 (rate = k[RCl][OH⁻]); D considers only the hydroxide ions.
items.why: C11.9 MCQs appear almost every session (Jan2026 Q3, Oct2025 Q3, Jun2025 Q11); linking the S_{N}1 rate equation to a rate-factor calculation is new.

items.name: Rate equations as evidence for SN1 and SN2 (primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes)
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.9 - that knowledge of the rate e
items.question: 1-bromopentane and 2-bromo-2-methylbutane are isomers of C₅H₁₁Br. Their skeletal formulae are shown. Each is hydrolysed by aqueous sodium hydroxide at 298 K, in a solvent of ethanol and water. The table shows initial-rate data for the two reactions. Deduce the order of reaction with respect to each reactant for the hydrolysis of 1-bromopentane. Justify your answers. Deduce the rate equation for the hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. Justify your answer. Explain how the rate equations for these two reactions provide evidence for the mechanisms of the hydrolysis of primary and tertiary halogenoalkanes. Include the mechanisms, using curly arrows, in your answer. Calculate the rate constant for the hydrolysis of 1-bromopentane. Give its units.
items.ms: Experiments 1 and 2: [C₅H₁₁Br] doubles at constant [OH⁻] and the rate doubles, so first order in 1-bromopentane Experiments 2 and 3: [OH⁻] triples at constant [C₅H₁₁Br] and the rate triples, so first order in OH⁻ Experiments 4 and 5: [C₅H₁₁Br] triples and the rate triples, so first order in 2-bromo-2-methylbutane; experiments 5 and 6: [OH⁻] doubles and the rate is unchanged, so zero order in OH⁻ rate = k[(CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃] IC1 1-bromopentane (primary): both the halogenoalkane and OH⁻ appear in the rate equation, so both are in the rate-determining step, which is the only step: SN2 IC2 SN2: the lone pair on O of OH⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of the C–Br bond, and the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically with Br⁻ leaving (curly arrows from the lone pair and from the C–Br bond) IC3 SN2 goes through a transition state with the O–C bond forming as the C–Br bond breaks, drawn in square brackets with the negative charge outside IC4 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (tertiary): only the halogenoalkane is in the rate equation, so OH⁻ is not in the rate-determining step and reacts in a later fast step: SN1 IC5 SN1: slow step, the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to give a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻; fast step, the lone pair of OH⁻ attacks the carbocation IC6 The tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect) / the alkyl groups hinder attack on the carbon, so tertiary reacts by SN1; a primary carbocation is too unstable and there is little hindrance, so primary reacts by SN2 k = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ ÷ (0.10 × 0.10) k = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (value and units)
items.why: C11.9 is warm (13 of 18 sessions) and has carried the paper's 6-mark question twice (Oct2021 Q18, Jan2025 Q18(a)); asking candidates to deduce both rate equations from data first is the fresh form.

items.name: Activation energy from experimental data (graphs and calculations)
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.10 - use calculations and graphic
items.question: Nitrogen dioxide decomposes at high temperature. 2NO₂(g) → 2NO(g) + O₂(g) A graph of ln k against 1/T for this reaction is a straight line with a gradient of −1.37 × 10⁴ K. ln k = −Ea/RT + constant R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ What is the activation energy of the reaction? −114 kJ mol⁻¹ +1.65 kJ mol⁻¹ +114 kJ mol⁻¹ +1.14 × 10⁵ kJ mol⁻¹
items.ms: Gradient = −Ea/R, so Ea = 1.37 × 10⁴ × 8.31 = 1.14 × 10⁵ J mol⁻¹ = +114 kJ mol⁻¹. A has the wrong sign; B divides by R instead of multiplying (in kJ); D is the value in J mol⁻¹ labelled as kJ mol⁻¹.
items.why: E_{a} from the gradient of ln k against 1/T is examined in most sessions (Jun2022 Q12, Oct2023 Q4, Oct2025 Q2); sign, R and kJ/J slips are the errors the examiner reports name most often.

items.name: Activation energy from experimental data (graphs and calculations)
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.10 - use calculations and graphic
items.question: The rate constant of a reaction was measured at several temperatures, with and without a catalyst. A graph of ln k against 1/T was plotted for each set of results. ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A Assume that the catalyst does not change the value of A. Compared with the line for the uncatalysed reaction, the line for the catalysed reaction is less steep and above it. parallel to it and above it. steeper and above it. less steep and below it.
items.ms: The catalyst lowers Ea, so the gradient (−Ea/R) is less negative: the line is less steep. With the same ln A (intercept at 1/T = 0), ln k is larger at every temperature, so the line lies above. B assumes the catalyst leaves Ea unchanged; C would mean a higher Ea; D would mean the catalyst slows the reaction.
items.why: That a catalyst lowers the activation energy is core C11.1 knowledge, but its effect on an Arrhenius plot (examined in 12 of 18 sessions) has never been asked; an MCQ is the likeliest form.

items.name: Activation energy from experimental data (graphs and calculations)
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.10 - use calculations and graphic
items.question: Di-tert-butyl peroxide (DTBP), (CH₃)₃COOC(CH₃)₃, is used to start polymerisation reactions. When it is heated in the gas phase, it decomposes. (CH₃)₃COOC(CH₃)₃(g) → 2CH₃COCH₃(g) + C₂H₆(g) The reaction was followed by measuring the total pressure of the gases in a sealed vessel of fixed volume at constant temperature. Pure DTBP was added to the vessel at time zero. Explain why measuring the total pressure can be used to follow this reaction. At 420 K, the initial pressure of DTBP was 30.0 kPa. After 40 minutes, the partial pressure of DTBP had fallen to 18.9 kPa. Calculate the total pressure in the vessel after 40 minutes. The graph shows how the partial pressure of DTBP changes with time at 420 K. Use the graph to show that the reaction is first order with respect to DTBP. Show your working on the graph. Calculate the rate constant at 420 K, in s⁻¹. [k = 0.693 ÷ t½] The rate constant is 5.41 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at 430 K and 3.72 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 450 K. ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Calculate the activation energy of the reaction, in kJ mol⁻¹. Predict the sign of ΔSsystem for the decomposition. Justify your answer. For the decomposition, ΔH = −177 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔSsystem = +370 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔStotal for the decomposition at 420 K. Use your value of Ea from (d) and the rate constant at 420 K to estimate the half-life of DTBP at 298 K. Give your answer in years. [1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s] Use your answers to (e)(ii) and (f) to explain why DTBP is described as thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable at room temperature. The first step of the mechanism is the breaking of the O–O bond. (CH₃)₃COOC(CH₃)₃ → 2(CH₃)₃CO• Explain why this step is consistent with the rate equation if it is the rate-determining step.
items.ms: 1 mol of gas forms 3 mol of gas, so the total pressure increases as the reaction proceeds (pressure is proportional to the amount of gas at constant volume and temperature) Pressure of DTBP decomposed = 30.0 − 18.9 = 11.1 kPa, forming 2 × 11.1 = 22.2 kPa of propanone and 11.1 kPa of ethane Total pressure = 18.9 + 22.2 + 11.1 = 52.2 kPa Two half-lives shown on the graph, e.g. 30 → 15 kPa and 15 → 7.5 kPa, each 60 min (58–62 min) The half-life is constant, so the reaction is first order t½ = 60 × 60 = 3600 s k = 0.693 ÷ 3600 = 1.93 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ ln k values −7.522 and −5.594 / ln(k₂/k₁) = 1.928 Ea = R × ln(k₂/k₁) ÷ (1/T₁ − 1/T₂) = 8.31 × 1.928 ÷ 1.03 × 10⁻⁴ Ea = +155 kJ mol⁻¹ Positive, because 1 mol of gas forms 3 mol of gas (so there are more ways of arranging the particles and their energy) ΔSsurroundings = −ΔH ÷ T = −(−177000) ÷ 420 = +421 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔStotal = 370 + 421 = +791 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ln(k₂₉₈ ÷ k₄₂₀) = −(Ea/R)(1/298 − 1/420) = −(155000 ÷ 8.31) × 9.75 × 10⁻⁴ = −18.2 k₂₉₈ = 1.93 × 10⁻⁴ × e−18.2 = 2.5 × 10⁻¹² s⁻¹ t½ = 0.693 ÷ k₂₉₈ = 2.8 × 10¹¹ s = 9.0 × 10³ years Thermodynamically unstable: ΔStotal is positive, so the decomposition is feasible (and, because ΔH is negative and ΔSsystem positive, it is feasible at all temperatures) Kinetically stable: the activation energy is high, so at 298 K very few molecules have energy ≥ Ea and the rate is negligible (half-life of thousands of years) Only one DTBP molecule takes part in this step, so rate = k[DTBP], first order as found in (c)(i)
items.why: C11.10 is the most heavily examined kinetics point (12 of 18 sessions, 4.8% of marks); the two-temperature calculation (Jan2023 Q17(b), Oct2022 Q16(c)) and the link between a high E_{a} and kinetic stability (Jan2020 Q18(b)) suit a synoptic Section C question built on pressure data.

items.name: Heterogeneous (solid) catalysts in gas-phase industrial reactions
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.11 - the use of a solid (heteroge
items.question: In the Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen react in the gas phase over a solid iron catalyst. N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) Describe how the solid iron catalyst increases the rate of the reaction. The iron catalyst is used as small porous pellets rather than as large lumps. Explain why.
items.ms: Nitrogen and hydrogen molecules are adsorbed onto the surface of the iron (at active sites) Bonds in the reactant molecules (e.g. N≡N) are weakened / the molecules are held close together, so the activation energy is lower The product, ammonia, is desorbed from the surface, freeing the sites The pellets have a larger surface area, so there are more sites where reactant molecules can be adsorbed (at the same time), giving a faster rate
items.why: C11.11 has been asked only once (Jun2021 Q16(c): adsorb, weaken, desorb); a gas-phase industrial context, unused for five years, makes a short question likely.

items.name: Core Practicals 9a and 9b: iodine–propanone titrimetric method; clock reaction
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.12 - CORE PRACTICALS 9a and 9b Following the rate
items.question: Peroxodisulfate ions oxidise iodide ions. S₂O₈²⁻(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2SO₄²⁻(aq) + I₂(aq) The rate of this reaction can be investigated using an iodine clock reaction. In each experiment, a student mixed 0.200 mol dm⁻³ potassium iodide solution, 5.0 cm³ of 0.00500 mol dm⁻³ sodium thiosulfate solution, 2.0 cm³ of starch solution and water in a beaker. The student then added 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ potassium peroxodisulfate solution, started a timer and recorded the time, t, for the colour of the mixture to change. The total volume of each mixture was 50.0 cm³. The thiosulfate ions react rapidly with iodine. I₂(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → 2I⁻(aq) + S₄O₆²⁻(aq) State the colour change at the end of each experiment. Explain how this method gives a measure of the initial rate of the reaction. Explain why water was added to each mixture so that the total volume was always 50.0 cm³. Calculate the initial rate of formation of iodine in mixture 1, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Deduce the order of reaction with respect to iodide ions and with respect to peroxodisulfate ions. Justify your answers using the data. Write the rate equation for the reaction and calculate the rate constant, k, using your answer to (d). Include units in your answer.
items.ms: Colourless to blue-black The iodine formed reacts immediately with the thiosulfate ions, so no iodine remains at first When all the thiosulfate has been used up, the iodine formed reacts with the starch to give the blue-black colour The same (fixed) amount of iodine has formed in time t in each experiment, so the rate is proportional to 1/t The amount of thiosulfate is small, so only a small fraction of the reactants is used up before the colour change and the concentrations hardly change: the rate is (close to) the initial rate So that the concentration of each reactant is proportional to the volume of its solution used / so that only the concentration of one reactant changes between experiments mol S₂O₃²⁻ = 5.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.00500 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ and mol I₂ = 2.50 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 2 = 1.25 × 10⁻⁵ [I₂] formed = 1.25 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 0.0500 = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ (mol dm⁻³) rate = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ 71 = 3.52 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ Mixtures 1, 2 and 3: halving / doubling the volume (concentration) of KI doubles / halves the time, so the rate is proportional to [I⁻]: first order in I⁻ Mixtures 1, 4 and 5: halving / doubling the volume of K₂S₂O₈ doubles / halves the time, so first order in S₂O₈²⁻ rate = k[S₂O₈²⁻][I⁻] In mixture 1: [I⁻] = 0.200 × 10.0 ÷ 50.0 = 0.0400 and [S₂O₈²⁻] = 0.0400 × 10.0 ÷ 50.0 = 8.00 × 10⁻³ (mol dm⁻³) k = 3.52 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ (0.0400 × 8.00 × 10⁻³) = 1.10 × 10⁻² dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
items.why: Core Practical 9b was the basis of Jan2023 Q17 and Jan2024 Q16 (hydrogen peroxide clock), and both ERs say candidates did not understand the principle; the peroxodisulfate clock with volumes to turn into concentrations is the obvious next variant.

items.name: Core Practical 10: activation energy
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 11 Kinetics
C11.13 - CORE PRACTICAL 10 Finding the activation energy of
items.question: A student used the reaction between magnesium ribbon and hydrochloric acid to find the activation energy of the reaction. Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) In each experiment, the student warmed 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid in a water bath, added a 2.0 cm length of magnesium ribbon, and measured the time, t, taken for the magnesium to disappear. Explain why 1/t can be used as a measure of the rate of reaction in these experiments. Explain why the hydrochloric acid is in large excess. Suggest how the student could make sure that the temperature recorded for each experiment is as accurate as possible. The table shows the student's results. Complete the table. Plot a graph of ln(1/t) against 1/T on the grid. Draw a line of best fit. Identify the anomalous result and suggest a reason for it. Since 1/t is proportional to the rate constant, k, ln(1/t) = −Ea/RT + constant R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ Use your graph to calculate the activation energy, Ea, of the reaction. Give your answer to three significant figures, with units. Another student did the same experiments using the same mass of magnesium powder instead of ribbon. State and explain the effect, if any, on the value of Ea obtained.
items.ms: The same amount (mass / length) of magnesium reacts in every experiment Rate = amount reacted ÷ time, so the rate is proportional to 1/t So that the acid concentration stays (almost) constant during each experiment and is the same in every experiment, so only the temperature affects the rate Measure the temperature of the acid just before adding the magnesium and again when it has disappeared, and use the mean / keep the reaction vessel in the water bath during the reaction 1/T at 50 °C = 3.096 × 10⁻³ (K⁻¹) ln(1/t) at 30 °C = −4.635 Axes the correct way round, labelled 1/T / K⁻¹ and ln(1/t), with a scale on which the points cover at least half the grid in each direction All six points plotted correctly (± half a small square) Straight line of best fit that ignores the anomalous point at 40 °C The 40 °C result (time too long / point below the line); e.g. the magnesium had an oxide coating / was not cleaned, or the acid cooled below 40 °C Gradient calculated from the line, using a large triangle, e.g. −5.8 × 10³ K (range −5.4 to −6.2 × 10³ K) Ea = −gradient × R Ea = +47.9 kJ mol⁻¹ (range 45–52), to 3 SF with units No effect: Ea is the same The larger surface area increases the rate by the same factor at every temperature, so every ln(1/t) value rises by the same amount and the gradient is unchanged / Ea depends on the reaction, not on the surface area
items.why: Core Practical 10 has been examined only through its data analysis (Jan2026 Q16, Jan2024 Q16(c)); the spec's suggested magnesium–acid version, with parts on why 1/t measures rate and on controlling variables, has not yet been set.

items.name: Kc expressions, homogeneous and heterogeneous
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria
C13.1 - deduce an expression for Kc
items.question: For the equilibrium H₂(g) + Br₂(g) ⇌ 2HBr(g) the equilibrium constant at 700 K is Kc = K. What is the value of Kc at 700 K for the equilibrium HBr(g) ⇌ ½H₂(g) + ½Br₂(g)? √K 1/K² 1/(2K) 1/√K
items.ms: Reversing the equation inverts Kc (1/K) and halving every coefficient takes the square root, so Kc = 1/√K. A takes the square root but does not invert; B squares instead of taking the square root; C halves the value instead of taking the square root.
items.why: Oct2020 doubled an equation and Jan2025 halved one (for Kp); reversing and halving together has not yet been asked.

items.name: Kc expressions, homogeneous and heterogeneous
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria
C13.1 - deduce an expression for Kc
items.question: Iron(II) ions react with silver ions in aqueous solution. A grey precipitate of silver forms and a dynamic equilibrium is set up. Fe²⁺(aq) + Ag⁺(aq) ⇌ Fe³⁺(aq) + Ag(s) Write the expression for the equilibrium constant, Kc, for this reaction and give its units.
items.ms: Kc = [Fe³⁺(aq)] / ([Fe²⁺(aq)][Ag⁺(aq)]) Units: dm³ mol⁻¹
items.why: C13.1 has come up in 11 of 18 sessions, nearly always for gases; an aqueous equilibrium with a solid product (the spec's Fe²⁺/Ag⁺ suggested practical) has not been used.

items.name: Kp expressions in partial pressures
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry

items.question: Sodium hydrogencarbonate in baking powder decomposes when heated. In a closed container the following equilibrium is set up. 2NaHCO₃(s) ⇌ Na₂CO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(g) Which gives the expression for Kp and its units? Kp = p(CO₂) × p(H₂O); units atm² Kp = p(CO₂) × p(H₂O) / p(NaHCO₃)²; no units Kp = p(Na₂CO₃) × p(CO₂) × p(H₂O) / p(NaHCO₃)²; units atm Kp = [CO₂][H₂O]; units mol² dm⁻⁶
items.ms: Solids do not appear in Kp, so Kp = p(CO₂) × p(H₂O) with units atm × atm = atm². B and C include partial pressures of the solids; D uses square brackets (concentrations), which describe Kc, not Kp.
items.why: C13.2 has come up in 16 of 18 sessions and Kp-with-solids MCQs recur (Oct2023, Oct2024); square brackets in Kp is the error the examiner reports name most often.

items.name: Calculating Kc and Kp (with units)
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria
C13.3 - calculate a value, with unit
items.question: Solid ammonium carbamate, H₂NCOONH₄, is placed in an evacuated flask at 313 K. It decomposes until the following equilibrium is set up. H₂NCOONH₄(s) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + CO₂(g) The total pressure at equilibrium is 0.240 atm. What is the value of Kp at 313 K? 1.73 × 10⁻³ atm³ 2.05 × 10⁻³ atm³ 1.28 × 10⁻² atm² 1.38 × 10⁻² atm³
items.ms: The gases form in the ratio 2 : 1, so p(NH₃) = ⅔ × 0.240 = 0.160 atm and p(CO₂) = ⅓ × 0.240 = 0.0800 atm. Kp = p(NH₃)² × p(CO₂) = 0.160² × 0.0800 = 2.05 × 10⁻³ atm³ (the solid is not included). A takes each partial pressure as half the total pressure; C does not square p(NH₃); D cubes the total pressure.
items.why: C13.3 is hot (16 of 18 sessions); a heterogeneous Kp found from the total pressure alone, with the gases in a fixed ratio, has not been asked.

items.question: 0.500 mol of sulfuryl chloride, SO₂Cl₂, was heated in a sealed 2.00 dm³ flask until equilibrium was reached. SO₂Cl₂(g) ⇌ SO₂(g) + Cl₂(g) The equilibrium mixture contained 0.150 mol of chlorine. What is the value of Kc? 1.61 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ 2.25 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ 3.21 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ 6.43 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³
items.ms: [SO₂] = [Cl₂] = 0.150 ÷ 2.00 = 0.0750 mol dm⁻³; [SO₂Cl₂] = (0.500 − 0.150) ÷ 2.00 = 0.175 mol dm⁻³; Kc = 0.0750² ÷ 0.175 = 3.21 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³. A uses the equilibrium moles of SO₂Cl₂ (0.350) without dividing by the volume; B uses the initial concentration of SO₂Cl₂ (0.250 mol dm⁻³); D uses moles throughout.
items.why: Kc from moles and volume recurs (Oct2022, Oct2023, Jun2025, Jan2026); the examiner reports single out initial moles and not dividing by the volume.

items.question: Methanol is manufactured from carbon monoxide and hydrogen over a copper–zinc oxide catalyst. Calculate the temperature at which ΔStotal = 0. State the value of the equilibrium constant, K, at this temperature. Justify your answer. The diagram shows a simplified flow scheme for the industrial process. Suggest why a high pressure is used and why the unreacted gases are recycled.
items.ms: Kp = p(CH₃OH) / (p(CO) × p(H₂)²) Equilibrium moles: CO = 0.370 and H₂ = 1.74 (mol) Total = 2.74 mol; mole fractions CO = 0.135, H₂ = 0.635, CH₃OH = 0.230 Partial pressures: p(CO) = 2.70 atm, p(H₂) = 12.7 atm, p(CH₃OH) = 4.60 atm Kp = 4.60 / (2.70 × 12.7²) = 1.06 × 10⁻² Units: atm⁻² V = nRT / p = 2.74 × 8.31 × 500 ÷ (2.03 × 10⁶) = 5.61 × 10⁻³ m³ = 5.61 dm³ Kc = (0.630/5.61) / ((0.370/5.61) × (1.74/5.61)²) = 17.7 dm⁶ mol⁻² Qp = 1.50 / (2.50 × 6.00²) = 1.67 × 10⁻² (atm⁻²) Qp is greater than Kp, so the mixture is not at equilibrium so the reaction goes to the left / some methanol decomposes into CO and H₂ until Qp = Kp Kp is smaller at 523 K because the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH negative), so a higher temperature favours the reverse (endothermic) reaction ΔStotal = ΔSsystem − ΔH/T = 0, so T = ΔH ÷ ΔSsystem = (−90700) ÷ (−219) T = 414 K K = 1, because ΔStotal = R ln K, and ln K = 0 when ΔStotal = 0 High pressure: there are fewer moles of gas on the right (3 → 1), so the equilibrium yield of methanol increases / the rate increases Recycling: only part of the CO and H₂ is converted in each pass (Kp is small at 523 K), so recycling gives a high overall conversion / avoids wasting reactants
items.why: C13.3 is the topic's biggest earner (6.7% of unit marks, 16 of 18 sessions) and moles → mole fraction → partial pressure → Kp recurs in long questions; methanol is a new context, and Kc via pV = nRT and a Qp test (both Oct2025) plus K = 1 when ΔS_total = 0 extend it synoptically.

items.question: Nickel(II) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide in a closed container. NiO(s) + CO(g) ⇌ Ni(s) + CO₂(g) ΔH = −43 kJ mol⁻¹ Which change increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the equilibrium mixture? adding more nickel(II) oxide increasing the temperature decreasing the volume of the container adding more carbon monoxide
items.ms: Adding CO raises the concentration of a reactant, so the equilibrium shifts to the right and more CO₂ forms. A: NiO is a solid, so adding more does not change the position of equilibrium. B: the forward reaction is exothermic, so raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left. C: there is one mole of gas on each side, so changing the pressure does not change the amounts.
items.why: C13.4 MCQs recur (Jan2022, Oct2022, Jan2024, Jan2025, Jun2025), mostly on temperature and pressure; the spec's 'how, if at all' for a heterogeneous system (adding more solid, equal moles of gas) has not been tested.

items.name: Effect of temperature, pressure and catalyst on composition
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria
C13.4 - how, if at all, a change in
items.question: Most hydrogen is manufactured by the steam reforming of methane. CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g) The graph shows how the percentage of methane converted at equilibrium varies with temperature at two different pressures, for a starting mixture of 3 mol of steam to 1 mol of methane. A typical plant uses a temperature of 1100 K, a pressure of 30 atm and a nickel catalyst. Discuss the choice of these conditions. Use the graph and the equation in your answer. Carbon can be deposited on the nickel catalyst by a side reaction. CH₄(g) ⇌ C(s) + 2H₂(g) Write the expression for Kc for this side reaction and give its units. Explain the effect, if any, of increasing the total pressure on the equilibrium amount of carbon deposited. Explain, in terms of Kp, why using a large excess of steam increases the percentage of methane converted in the main reaction.
items.ms: IC1 The graph shows that the percentage converted increases with temperature, so the forward reaction is endothermic IC2 1100 K gives a high equilibrium conversion (about 70% at 30 atm) and a high rate, so for temperature there is no conflict between rate and yield IC3 The temperature is limited by the energy (fuel) cost and the materials of the reactor; the curves level off at high temperature, so further heating gives little extra conversion IC4 There are 2 mol of gas on the left and 4 mol on the right, so a higher pressure lowers the equilibrium conversion (about 70% at 30 atm against about 91% at 10 atm) IC5 30 atm is still used as a compromise: the higher pressure increases the rate / allows a smaller plant / delivers the hydrogen at pressure so less compression is needed later IC6 The nickel catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative route with a lower activation energy, but does not change Kp or the equilibrium conversion Kc = [H₂]² / [CH₄] mol dm⁻³ There is 1 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol of gas on the right (carbon is a solid and is not counted) so the equilibrium shifts to the left and less carbon is deposited Kp = p(CO) × p(H₂)³ / (p(CH₄) × p(H₂O)) is constant at constant temperature / is not changed by adding steam Increasing p(H₂O) increases the denominator, so the quotient / Qp becomes smaller than Kp so more methane reacts / the equilibrium shifts to the right until the quotient equals Kp again
items.why: C13.4 has come up in 12 of 18 sessions (Haber, contact and ethanol processes, all exothermic); an endothermic process with more gas moles on the right, where temperature needs no compromise, has not been asked, and equilibrium conditions have filled the 6-mark slot before (Oct2020).

items.question: Carbon monoxide reacts with chlorine to form phosgene, COCl₂. CO(g) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ COCl₂(g) More chlorine is added to an equilibrium mixture at constant temperature and volume. Which row shows the effect on Kc and on the amount of carbon monoxide when equilibrium is re-established? Kc increases; amount of CO decreases Kc does not change; amount of CO decreases Kc does not change; amount of CO increases Kc decreases; amount of CO does not change
items.ms: Kc depends only on temperature, so it does not change. Adding Cl₂ makes the quotient [COCl₂]/([CO][Cl₂]) smaller than Kc, so CO reacts with Cl₂ until the quotient equals Kc again: the amount of CO decreases. A and D wrongly change Kc; C has the shift in the wrong direction.
items.why: C13.5 has come up in 10 of 18 sessions, for pressure, temperature, surface area or a catalyst; a change in concentration, which the spec also names, has not yet been the change asked about.

items.question: Calcium carbonate is heated in a closed cylinder fitted with a gas-tight piston, as shown in the diagram, until equilibrium is reached. CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g) At 1100 K, Kp = 0.86 atm. The piston is pushed in so that the volume of gas is halved. The temperature stays at 1100 K and some of each solid remains. Explain, in terms of Kp, what happens to the partial pressure of carbon dioxide and to the amount of calcium carbonate in the cylinder.
items.ms: Kp = p(CO₂) (solids not included) and its value does not change because the temperature is constant Halving the volume (initially) doubles p(CO₂), so p(CO₂) / Qp is now greater than Kp So CO₂ reacts with CaO / the equilibrium shifts to the left, and the amount of CaCO₃ increases until p(CO₂) equals Kp again, so the final partial pressure of CO₂ is 0.86 atm, the same as before
items.why: C13.5 has come up in 10 of 18 sessions, almost only as MCQs; the 'in terms of Kp' explanation (Oct2020) is the digest's top beyond-spec item and has never been set for a heterogeneous system.

items.name: Effect of temperature on K, exothermic and endothermic
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria

items.question: Carbon dioxide reacts with hydrogen in the reverse water–gas shift reaction. CO₂(g) + H₂(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂O(g) ΔH = +41 kJ mol⁻¹ Which change increases the value of Kp? adding a catalyst increasing the total pressure increasing the partial pressure of hydrogen increasing the temperature
items.ms: Only temperature changes Kp. The forward reaction is endothermic, so Kp increases as the temperature increases. A catalyst (A), pressure (B) and the partial pressure of a reactant (C) do not change Kp.
items.why: C13.6 is hot (14 of 18 sessions); 'which change increases Kp' (May2024, Jan2025) has only been set for the exothermic Haber process.

path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria

items.question: For the equilibrium PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) ⇌ PCl₅(g) Kc = 25.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ at 523 K and Kc = 2.00 dm³ mol⁻¹ at 600 K. Which row gives Kc at 600 K for the decomposition PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) and the sign of ΔH for the decomposition? 0.0400 mol dm⁻³; ΔH positive 0.500 mol dm⁻³; ΔH negative 0.500 mol dm⁻³; ΔH positive 2.00 dm³ mol⁻¹; ΔH negative
items.ms: The decomposition is the reverse reaction, so Kc = 1 ÷ 2.00 = 0.500 mol dm⁻³. Kc for the combination falls as the temperature rises, so the combination is exothermic and the decomposition is endothermic (ΔH positive). A inverts the 523 K value; B has the wrong sign of ΔH; D does not invert Kc and gives the sign for the combination.
items.why: Oct2021 asked how forward and reverse K change with temperature; deducing the sign of ΔH from two K values and inverting K for the reverse reaction has not been asked.

items.name: Effect of temperature on K, exothermic and endothermic
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria

items.question: Chlorine can be recovered from waste hydrogen chloride by the Deacon process, using a copper(II) chloride catalyst. 4HCl(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2Cl₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) The table shows the value of Kp for this equilibrium at different temperatures. The graph shows the percentage of hydrogen chloride converted at equilibrium at 1 atm, for a starting mixture of 4 mol of HCl to 1 mol of O₂. Write the expression for Kp for this reaction and deduce its units. Use the data to deduce the sign of the enthalpy change, ΔH, for the forward reaction. Justify your answer. The equation for the reverse reaction is 2Cl₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) ⇌ 4HCl(g) + O₂(g) Calculate the value of Kp for the reverse reaction at 700 K. Include units in your answer. State how the value of Kp for the reverse reaction changes as the temperature is increased. Give a reason for your answer. The industrial process is operated at about 700 K. Use the table and the graph to explain why a temperature of 700 K is used rather than 500 K or 900 K.
items.ms: Kp = p(Cl₂)² × p(H₂O)² / (p(HCl)⁴ × p(O₂)) atm⁻¹ Kp decreases as the temperature increases / the percentage converted falls as the temperature rises so the forward reaction is exothermic / ΔH is negative Kp = 1 ÷ 64 = 1.6 × 10⁻² atm It increases, because the reverse reaction is endothermic At 500 K, Kp is very large / about 93% is converted, but the rate is too slow (even with the catalyst) At 900 K, the rate is fast but Kp is small / only about 52% is converted At 700 K, Kp (64 atm⁻¹) is still large / about 74% is converted at an acceptable rate, so 700 K is a compromise between yield and rate
items.why: C13.6 is hot (14 of 18 sessions) but nearly always a one-mark MCQ; the Deacon process is a new context, and reading K against temperature with a yield graph brings in C13.9 (cool) and catalysts (C11.11).

items.name: Temperature affects position through the value of K
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria
C13.7 - that the effect of temperature on the positio
items.question: Dinitrogen tetroxide, N₂O₄, is a colourless gas. It dissociates to form nitrogen dioxide, NO₂, a brown gas. N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) A sealed glass tube contains an equilibrium mixture of the two gases. At 298 K, the equilibrium partial pressures are p(N₂O₄) = 0.750 atm and p(NO₂) = 0.335 atm. Calculate the value of Kp at 298 K. Include units in your answer. At 330 K, Kp = 1.3 atm. Deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Justify your answer. The tube is moved from a water bath at 298 K into a water bath at 330 K. When the gas has just reached 330 K, before its composition has changed, the partial pressures are p(N₂O₄) = 0.831 atm and p(NO₂) = 0.371 atm. By calculating the value of p(NO₂)²/p(N₂O₄) at this moment, explain what happens to the position of equilibrium and to the colour of the mixture as it reaches equilibrium at 330 K. A student wrote: 'Heating the mixture moves the equilibrium to the right, and this makes Kp increase.' Explain why the student's statement is incorrect.
items.ms: Kp = p(NO₂)² / p(N₂O₄) = 0.335² / 0.750 = 0.150 atm Endothermic / ΔH is positive because Kp increases as the temperature increases (so the forward reaction is favoured at higher temperature) Qp = p(NO₂)²/p(N₂O₄) = 0.371² / 0.831 = 0.166 (atm) Qp is less than Kp at 330 K (1.3 atm), so p(NO₂) must increase / p(N₂O₄) must decrease until Qp = Kp so the equilibrium position moves to the right (more NO₂ forms) and the mixture becomes darker brown The temperature change itself changes (increases) Kp; the equilibrium then moves to the right because Kp has increased, so that the quotient equals the new Kp (the shift is the result, not the cause)
items.why: C13.7 has been asked once in 18 sessions (Jan2022) and never with numbers; a quotient after heating makes 'temperature acts through K' testable, using the spec's N₂O₄/NO₂ suggested practical.

items.question: For the cracking of ethane at 800 K, C₂H₆(g) ⇌ C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) Kp = 2.3 × 10⁻³ atm What is the total entropy change, ΔStotal, for this reaction at 800 K? [R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹] −50.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ −21.9 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ −0.731 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ +50.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
items.ms: ΔStotal = R ln K = 8.31 × ln (2.3 × 10⁻³) = 8.31 × (−6.07) = −50.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. B uses log₁₀ instead of ln; C divides ln K by R; D has the wrong sign (K less than 1 gives a negative ΔStotal).
items.why: K from ΔS_total was asked in Jan2021 (MCQ) and Jan2022; ΔS_total from K has only appeared inside a long question (Jun2021), and ΔS_total = R ln K is never given.

items.name: ΔStotal = R ln K and temperature
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria
C13.8 - the effect of a change in te
items.question: Nitrogen monoxide, NO, forms in car engines when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperature. N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g) The table shows values of the equilibrium constant, Kc, for this reaction at different temperatures. Write the expression for Kc for this reaction and explain why Kc has no units. Complete the table. Plot a graph of ln Kc (vertical axis) against 1/T (horizontal axis) on the grid. Draw a line of best fit. The gradient of the line is equal to −ΔH/R, where R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Use your graph to determine the enthalpy change, ΔH, for the forward reaction, in kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the total entropy change, ΔStotal, for the reaction at 2000 K. Use your answers to (d) and (e) in this part. Calculate the entropy change of the surroundings, ΔSsurroundings, at 2000 K. Hence calculate the entropy change of the system, ΔSsystem. Explain, in terms of ΔStotal, why the value of Kc increases as the temperature increases. At 298 K, Kc = 4.2 × 10⁻³¹. State what this value shows about the reaction between nitrogen and oxygen in air at 298 K.
items.ms: Kc = [NO]² / ([N₂][O₂]) The units (mol dm⁻³)² on the top and the bottom cancel / there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side 1/T at 2250 K = 4.44 × 10⁻⁴ (K⁻¹) ln Kc = −9.43 at 1750 K and −6.68 at 2250 K Axes labelled ln Kc and (1/T) / K⁻¹, with scales that use at least half of the grid in each direction All five points plotted correctly (to within half a small square) Straight line of best fit through the points Gradient from a large triangle on the line, e.g. (−5.71 − (−11.50)) ÷ (4.00 × 10⁻⁴ − 6.67 × 10⁻⁴) = −2.17 × 10⁴ (K) ΔH = −gradient × R = 2.17 × 10⁴ × 8.31 = 1.80 × 10⁵ J mol⁻¹ ΔH = +180 kJ mol⁻¹ (positive sign and units needed) ΔStotal = R ln Kc = 8.31 × ln (3.77 × 10⁻⁴) = 8.31 × (−7.88) = −65.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔSsurroundings = −ΔH/T = −180000 ÷ 2000 = −90.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔSsystem = ΔStotal − ΔSsurroundings = −65.5 − (−90.0) = +24.5 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ΔH is positive, so ΔSsurroundings (= −ΔH/T) is negative As T increases, ΔSsurroundings becomes less negative / smaller in magnitude, while ΔSsystem hardly changes so ΔStotal increases (becomes less negative), and as ΔStotal = R ln K, ln Kc and so Kc increase Kc is very small, so the equilibrium lies very far to the left / (virtually) no NO forms
items.why: C13.8 has come up in 8 of 18 sessions and the ln K against 1/T graph (Oct2022 Q18(c), 12 marks) is one of the digest's top beyond-spec items; ΔS_total = R ln K must be recalled, and NO from car engines is a new context.

items.name: Using K to judge the extent of reaction
path: Unit 4 Rates, Equilibria and Further Organic Chemistry
Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria
C13.9 - apply knowledge of the value
items.question: For the reaction of hydrogen with oxygen at 298 K, 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2H₂O(g) Kp = 1.4 × 10⁸⁰ atm⁻¹ A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can be stored at 298 K for years with no detectable formation of water. Explain what the value of Kp shows about this reaction, and why the mixture does not react at 298 K.
items.ms: Kp is very large, so the position of equilibrium lies very far to the right / the reaction would go almost to completion Kp gives no information about rate: the activation energy is (very) high, so the rate at 298 K is negligible / the mixture is kinetically stable
items.why: C13.9 is cool (4 of 18 sessions) and the Jun2023 report says most candidates did not comment on the size of K; linking a huge K with a negligible rate (kinetic stability, C12.11) has not been asked.
